REPORT OF BOARD OF ENGINEERS ON TRANSPORT
subsubtopic: FACILITIES-STATEMENT AS TO CAUSEWAY AND LOCK STRUCTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the report on the problem of crossing the strait of Canso.
On September 15, 1950, a meeting was held in my office for the purpose of considering the plans and specifications of the low-level bridge prepared by the consulting engineer, Dr. P. L. Pratley. This meeting was attended by the members of the board of engineers of the strait of Canso and by representatives of both the Canadian National Railways and the department of highways and public works of the province of Nova Scotia. At this meeting it was disclosed that engineers of both the railway and the province were of the opinion that the low-level bridge as designed was not practicable, and that they could not approve such a project.
As a result I immediately reconvened the Canso board of engineers with instructions that, in the light of the discussions, they review their previous findings and recommend the best method of improving the present rail and highway facilities across the strait. I am now in receipt of the report of the reconvened board.
The report indicates that further studies were made of two projects, one of which involved improvements to the existing ferry service, and the other the construction of a causeway and lock structure. The board advise that their estimate of cost of replacing the existing railway ferry service at
present capacity would be $9 million, which figure would be increased to $13,400,000 if present capacity were to be increased by provision of larger vessels and wider ferry slips. The estimate of cost of replacement of the highway ferry service amounts to $1,287,000, or a total estimated capital expenditure for combined services of $14,687,-
000.	As to the annual operating costs as estimated for these services, the board states that the operation of the railway ferry service would require $1,587,000 and the highway ferry service $370,000, making a combined total annual operating cost of $1,957,000.
The board also reports that, in reviewing their previous findings on the causeway and lock structure, their chief object was to search for ways and mqans to reduce the probable cost. They are now of the opinion that the best site is that of the low-level bridge at Balache point as proposed in the March, 1949, report. They propose a causeway which would be entirely built of rock placed by dump-trucks working from west to east. The slopes on this causeway would be finished at about the proportion of 1 vertical to 1J horizontal, and a lock of Welland ship canal dimensions but with sliding gates would be located on the Cape Breton end of the causeway. The railway and highway diversions would be similar to those as originally proposed for the low-level bridge.
In conclusion the board reports that in view of the elimination of the bridge projects and the high cost of improving the ferry services, the causeway scheme remains as the only practical solution to the problem. The capital cost of the causeway and lock is estimated by the board at $22,760,000 and the annual operating charge at $1,130,000.
I now table the report.

subtopic: INVITATION TO SEND OBSERVERS TO SEPTEMBER SESSION
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister, of which I have given him notice. It has to do with Mr. Speaker's announcement to the house on Monday that he had received a communication from the president of the consultative assembly of the Council of Europe, inviting this parliament to send observers to the session of the council commencing September 24 next. Will the Prime Minister state what action the government may take concerning this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INVITATION TO SEND OBSERVERS TO SEPTEMBER SESSION
speechtext:
It was some minutes after ten o'clock when the hon. member telephoned to my office in this connection. Had I had more time to do so, I would have prepared a carefully worded statement to answer the question, but I think hon. members would prefer to have it answered less formally and immediately.
This is an invitation which you, sir, stated had been addressed not to the government of Canada but to the parliament of Canada. Of course if the invitation were to be accepted I imagine that there would have to be some provision made for the expenses of any delegation that would go there representing this parliament, and that the government would have to take the responsibility of making the required recommendation to parliament. Because of that, and because of the interest which naturally attaches to this matter, it has been under consideration by the government, but no decision has yet been reached. There are many factors about which we are seeking to obtain more enlightenment. We are in communication with our representatives, both in London and in Washington, in that regard.
One of the factors to which consideration has to be given is the apparent fact that this Council of Europe is made up not of representatives of the governments of the countries but of the national groups of several countries in Europe. This may be all to the good, but it is somewhat of a departure, because what they would be doing is something which would have a profound effect upon the foreign policies of the governments of all those countries. According to the manner in which our parliamentary institutions are set up, foreign policy is usually a responsibility of the government of the country, and is usually handled through the foreign office of

the country. It would seem that this is a new way of going into matters that are of such great concern to the peoples and the governments of all the free countries of the world.
There is another matter which has given us some concern, and that is that the form of the invitation to this parliament seems to differ from the form of invitation extended to the houses of the United States congress. They have been invited to appoint a delegation to meet a delegation of the Council of Europe, and to have discussions with that delegation; whilst the invitation to this parliament, through you, sir, has been to send observers to attend the sittings of the council itself. We are curious to know if that is an intentional difference, or if it is just an accidental difference in the wording of the invitation. If it is intentional, we should like to know why the distinction is being made. We are also trying to ascertain whether invitations similar to the one addressed to this parliament have been sent to the parliaments of other commonwealth countries.
There is also the factor that it is nominally a council of Europe. For a long time there has been a Pan-American union of the republics of the western hemisphere, and they have never had observers from elsewhere attending their meetings. As a matter of fact we have not, because of our monarchical traditions, been included in that group. If the council has for its purpose the setting up of a federation of European states, I would say that we had no observers attending the Charlottetown or Quebec conferences at the time we were discussing our confederation, or at the time we were discussing union with Newfoundland. We are seeking to explore all these possible implications of the invitation that has been addressed to this parliament.
There would be some rather inconvenient features, in view of the fact that this meeting is scheduled for September 24, and we are contemplating an important session of our own parliament early in October. But that would probably not be an insuperable difficulty, nor would the difficulty arising from the fact that at that time of the year we usually have to provide a representative delegation to the meeting of the United Nations.
These are matters about which we have not yet obtained all the information and enlightenment we would wish to have before deciding to recommend an appropriation to parliament for official participation in the activities of this body. But the meeting will be taking place before parliament reconvenes; and if it is felt that we should take
Inquiries of the Ministry the responsibility of a recommendation to parliament, in supplementaries or otherwise when parliament reconvenes, I would expect that it should be a delegation representative of the complexion of the house and not merely a delegation representing the government party in the house; and I would expect to discuss it with the leader of the opposition.

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARIES AND NUMBERS OF JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks before we go into committee on this bill, because to me it is a most important measure. I feel that the administration of justice, and the manner in which we treat the judiciary of Canada, goes to the very root of the foundations of our democracies. Magna Carta, which is still part of the law of the commonwealth countries, including Canada, is often quoted in the house.
In Canada one of the things in which we take greatest pride is the impartial administration of justice, and the high type of the members of the judiciary; for it is fundamental to the well-being of every nation that all the citizens of a country have due respect for law and constituted authority.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) on Monday last, speaking about amendments to the Criminal Code, repeated the oft-quoted statement that under British justice a man is deemed to be innocent until he is proven guilty. As we know, that is not the law of all countries. But to uphold that principle in Canada, we must continue to have a capable and competent bench to administer the law.
So far as respect for law and authority in Canada is concerned, I believe that Canadians, perhaps more than people in other countries, have every reason to be proud of the administration of law and justice in this country. Under our set-up, in administering the law all judges must follow legal precedents. They also must follow a code of interpretation in their administration of the law, one which has been established for generations. These precedents are binding upon them. They must obey and follow the judgments of superior courts.

Judges must also take into consideration changing law to meet changing conditions. To guide them they have a mass of precedents from courts of record. This is not so in connection with committees or commissions. During the war, for instance, a rentals administrator was appointed to deal with problems affecting real property. Very often administrators of this type, who had never studied law, and had no knowledge of it, with the exception of the acts they were to interpret, were given power to interpret the law. In many cases judgments given on one day would be entirely opposite from those given the day following, in exactly similar circumstances. Under this procedure there does not seem to be any way of checking such things, but in my opinion the results did not add either to efficiency or to respect for law.
In Ontario we have a municipal board which administers and deals with a wide variety of legal matters. The members of the board, with the possible exception of the chairman, are not members of the legal profession. They have not had the long experience that judicial officers have had. The workmen's compensation board is another example. Then, if we want to take an example from the federal field, there is the wartime prices and trade board, in almost every branch of which there are people engaged in interpreting the law, for the enactment of which they themselves are responsible.
One of the fundamental principles of British justice is that there shall be a distinguishing difference between the judge, the prosecuting attorney, the jury, the witnesses, the plaintiff and the defendant; and we must bear that always in mind. We should make sure that all those appointed to high positions on the bench are able to perform in a capable manner the functions thereof. Therefore it naturally follows in my opinion that these men should be paid adequate salaries, in view of the importance of the high office they hold.
As I suggested yesterday to the Minister of Justice, if proper consideration had been given to the amendments introduced in 1946, at which time the salaries of judges were increased, it would not have been necessary to bring this bill before the house. Even at this late date I suggest to the Minister of Justice that the provision he has made for county and district court judges should be reviewed, because I think he will find that the increase is not sufficient. I think the minister will agree that the salaries paid to county court judges, and perhaps the salaries to be paid, are completely out of line with
Judges Act
salaries paid to others for work which is, if anything, of less importance to the community.
Yesterday the minister referred to New York state, where county court judges having comparable jurisdiction are paid a minimum of $16,000 per annum.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARIES AND NUMBERS OF JUDGES
speechtext: Does the hon. member recommend that we pay county court judges in Canada $16,000?

subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARIES AND NUMBERS OF JUDGES
speechtext:
No, I
am not even suggesting that. I am only pointing out that judges in New York state having practically the same jurisdiction are paid at a much higher rate. I am not suggesting at all that they should be paid $16,000.
Judges of the Supreme Court of Canada are paid not quite but almost double the salaries of county court judges. May I point out to the minister that, having regard to the volume of work done, and the importance of the respective courts to the public, it seems to me that so far as Ontario is concerned there is no practical reason why the county court judges should not be paid at the same rate as the supreme court judges, because, in Ontario at least, the work of county court judges has greatly increased throughout the year. Only recently their jurisdiction was increased, thereby increasing their work; and I believe that in the very near future there will be a further increase in the jurisdiction of the county court, thus further increasing the work.
I listened yesterday to the observations of hon. members who are not members of the legal profession and, while I have no criticism of what they said-it is their right and privilege to speak-there are certain matters with which they dealt and with which, after some years of experience, I am familiar. May I place these facts before the minister. Naturally I am more familiar with my county and the surrounding ones than I am with other jurisdictions. However, what I shall say about the county of Hastings can be applied with equal force to practically every other county in Ontario.
The county of Hastings is the largest in Ontario, with a population of well over 80,000, and is increasing every year. It consists of thirty-five municipalities, one town with a population of well over 10,000, and a city with a population of 27,000, as well as several other smaller towns and villages. Many years ago, when I began practising in the county, the population was not anything like what it is today. At that time there were two county court judges and, in addition, the local master of the supreme court. Today there is only one county court judge.

Judges Act
and there is no local master. The county court judge now handles and hears all matters that formerly came before the local master of the supreme court.
In my county there are twelve division courts, and in 1950, the last year for which there is a record, the county court judge spent seventy-three days in dealing with division court actions alone. The city of Belleville division court handled 1,379 cases. In addition, they had 133 judgment summonses and some fifty transcripts from other courts. The number of writs issued in the county court in * 1950 was 131, and the approximate number in 1951 will exceed 200, thus giving some indication of the greatly increased amount of work in the county court.
I have before me a list of the county court non-jury cases scheduled for hearing in April, 1951. There were fourteen cases set down for trial, and all fourteen were heard. I also have a list of cases set down for the general sessions of the peace and jury sittings held in June of this year. I find there were four criminal cases, two charges of perjury, one of bigamy, and one of theft. All cases were heard. There were five jury cases and eight non-jury cases. I point out that the average jury case takes practically two days and a non-jury case one day. The county court judge naturally hears all motions and other matters pertaining to county court actions. In addition, the county court judge handles a large number of matters relating to actions in the supreme court. In one year the county court judge of my county will hear from fifty to seventy-five motions pertaining to supreme court matters. Up to the middle of April of this year twenty-seven such motions had been heard. I would point out to the minister that there are many cases heard in the county court as the result of consent being given to the jurisdiction of that court inasmuch as the amount involved is beyond the statutory limit set for the county court.
I have referred to motions heard by the county court judge in his capacity as local judge of the supreme court. On one motion in which I was interested it took two full days to hear the argument. I know the average motion does not take anything like two days, but that is an indication of the time that is spent on certain matters. In addition, in the various county towns one week of five sitting days is usually allotted for the supreme court. It has become the practice, at least in my county, that cases which are not heard by the supreme court judge are, by his direction, handed over to

the county court judge, and I have noticed from the press that a number of supreme court cases have been heard by the county court judge.
In addition to all these various matters, the county court judge hears appeals from magistrates' decisions. He handles mechanics lien actions, and I noticed in the papers recently that there were no less than fifty-two naturalization applications to be heard before him. In addition to all these cases, there are innumerable provincial acts which provide for reference >or appeal to the local county court judge. I should like to refer to a few of them: the Adoption Act, the Agricultural Societies Act, the Assessment Act, the Bills of Sale and Chattel Mortgages Act, the Bonus Limitation Act, the Bulk Sales Act, the Cemetery Act, the Children of Unmarried Parents Act, the Conditional Sales Act, the Children's Protection Act, the Costs of Distress Act, the County Courts Act, the County Judges Act, the Creditors Relief Act, the Dependents Relief Act, the Ditches and Water Courses Act, the Division Courts Act, ithe Election Act, the Farm Loans Act, the Fraudulent Debtors Arrest Act, the High Schools Act, the Highway Improvement Act, the Highway Traffic Act, the House of Refuge Act, the Industrial Schools Act, the Judicature Act, the Jurors Act, the Juvenile and Family Courts Act, the Lakes and Rivers Improvement Act, the Line Fences Act, the Liquor Control Act, the Landlord and Tenant Act, the Local Improvements Act, the Master and Servants Act, the Mechanics Lien Act, the Mental Hospitals Act, the Money Lenders Act, the Municipal Act, the Municipal Drainage Act, the Notaries Act, the Partnership Act, the Power Commission Act, the Provincial Land Tax Act, the Public Schools Act, the Public Works Act, the Police Act, the Railways Act, the Registration of Deeds Act, the Property of Religious Institutions Act, the School Sites Act, the Separate Schools Act, the Snow Roads and Fences Act, the Succession Duty Act, the Surrogate Courts Act, the Trustee Act, the Vendors and Purchasers Act, the Voters Lists Act, the Wages Act, the Woodmen's Lien for Wages Act.
In addition to all these provincial acts, there are a certain number of federal statutes under which certain matters are referred to the local county court judge. In my county there is a full time court reporter, and it has been found that he is unable to handle the volume of work. He has had to have an assistant appointed. As was pointed out yesterday, in the smaller centres the judge is often regarded as the first citizen of the community. He

must necessarily give very freely of his time, and like all other citizens he is expected to support every worthy cause.
There are many other duties that the county judges perform of which the minister is well aware. I for one certainly feel that the men who are appointed to these posts, and who are cut off from earning additional salary in any way, should be paid a salary large enough to compensate them for the services they perform, and they should not have to be constantly worried over financial matters. Yesterday an hon. member from British Columbia referred to a judge in his province who, in order to educate his children, had to resign and go back to practice. I should like to tell the minister about a county court judge in my district who, when the salary was $5,000, came to see me about his son who was at law school. His daughter was also taking training in a hospital. The judge told me that at that time he had borrowed every cent he could on his insurance policies in order to finance the education of the boy at law school and to assist his daughter, and that it was absolutely impossible for him to continue on the salary he was receiving and keep the boy at law school. Despite all that was said yesterday by various members, I do not think that anybody in Canada expects or desires that the members of our judiciary should be constantly worried over financial matters.
In support of that I would like to read part of an editorial that appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of April 17:
Neither are judges' salaries substantial when measured against their responsibilities. The courts stand guard over the rights and liberties of every Canadian. We expect from them the highest standards of wisdom, of integrity, of independence. Judges must be, in a very real sense, above the common level; above the passions and anxieties of everyday life.
It is a great distinction to be a judge. Because of that, many lawyers have sacrificed their financial interests, and those of their dependents, to enter the judiciary. But it is not fair to expect them to do so; it is not fair to reward such men with little more than prestige. They should be enabled to live on a scale at least comparable with that they would otherwise have enjoyed.
This is not merely in their own interest; it is in the public's interest as well. If the law is to be maintained, if justice is to be dispensed in accordance with our proudest traditions; the ablest lawyers must be attracted to the bench; and once there, sustained in a manner befitting their duties and their abilities. We can economize on many things, but not on this. When it comes to justice, we can afford nothing but the best.
I suggest to the minister that the sentiments and thoughts there set out sum up the whole matter.
I have tried in a brief and general way to state some of the many and varied duties
Judges Act
performed by the average county court judge. Some may say that what applies in my county does not apply elsewhere. So far as the county of Peterborough is concerned, which adjoins my own, I know from personal experience that the same conditions exist there.
I would like to say just a word in regard to the uncalled-for comments made yesterday as to the political affiliations of judges prior to their appointment. In my district we have a system under which the four county court judges rotate. At the present time, as it happens, all four judges were formerly Liberals and were appointed by this government. But after the long years I have practised, and especially after the twelve years I have been a member of this house, I have no hesitation in saying that in appearing before those judges who prior to their appointment were of a political faith different from mine, I have never had the slightest cause even to suspect that by reason of political affiliation any discrimination of any kind was made against me. In fact, in fairness to those men I should say that I have often felt they leaned over backwards a long way in order to be fair in any matter with which I was connected.
I suggest to the minister again that he is making an error in the scale of salaries he is fixing for the county court judges. If he feels that he cannot increase their scale to that of the supreme court judges, I do suggest that the amount a county court judge receives should not be less than $10,000 a year. As I said before, and as I think the minister will agree, the adjustment made at this time will fix the salary for a long time to come; and I am sure that when this is through the minister will want to feel that he has made an adjustment which will be satisfactory both to the public and to those who will receive this increase. I suggest that even at this late date the minister reconsider the matter and bring in an amendment to the bill to provide that the county court judges shall receive not less than $10,000 a year.

I
wish to say a few words on this motion for second reading. Yesterday the house by vote made a definite decision on the measure; consequently I shall not delay matters unduly this morning. I would like to make it clear that I give place to no member of this house in my respect for the judges of our country and the positions they hold. It is largely because I respect the judges that I object to their being made a privileged class, with privileges to which very few in this country

Judges Act
can aspire-and not only privileges for themselves, but for their families as well, which I do not think is at all in accord with our democracy.
Yesterday the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) referred to Judge Wilson, of Prince George, who, as he said, found it necessary to resign his position in order to educate his family; and I believe that matter was also referred to by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White). At the moment I do not know just what salary this judge was receiving; but if a judge, getting whatever salary goes with that position, cannot educate his family, then God help the great majority of the families of Canada, because at that rate they can hope for no education at all. If a person cannot educate his children on $5,000 or $6,000 or $10,000 a year, what about those who do not receive $1,000 a year? What is going to happen to their families? What is really happening is that a small class in this country are able to educate their children so that those children may and do follow them in these high positions, while the rest are hewers of wood and drawers of water. As long as we accentuate that relationship instead of diminishing it, ve are not doing the best we can and should tor our country.
I said I honour and respect the judges and the positions they hold. I honour and respect them not only as judges but as men, and I honour and respect mankind as a whole: the farmer who tills the fields, the miner who takes his life in his hands in order to bring coal out of the mine, the lumberman who works in the forests, the men who carry on the dangerous operations of our railways. Surely we should respect these men and make provision for them after they have done their part in producing the wealth of this country and in building its capital; for I can tell hon. members that the capital of this country consists of the wages the workers earned but did not get. If we do not make fairly decent provision for the great mass of the people-and we are not doing that today-why should we make luxurious provision for the judges and their wives? I have not received any answer to that. Let me say again that I give place to no one in this house in my regard for the judicial institutions of my country and the persons who hold judgeships.
Yesterday the minister made the point-I think I am right in saying this-that the lower court judges had received only one increase since 1920. I think that speaks for itself. I believe it just shows that their position as of 1920 was so much better than that of the average citizen that it was neither necessary nor desirable to give them

an increase. Then the minister referred to the representations made by Percy Bengough, president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, on behalf of the judges. I am sure that it will be a great joy to Percy Bengough to know that anything he presented to the government has received attention, because to my knowledge Percy Bengough and the whole executive of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada have been making submissions to this government for years, and this is the first time in my twenty-one years in the house that I have heard any minister speak with approbation of the requests made by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.

All right, then; I am going to give you something to improve upon. I have in my hand a memorandum presented to the government of Canada by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada on Tuesday, April 10, 1951. I wonder if the minister remembers what this memorandum contains? Did he read it, or has he forgotten it already, or was he there when it was presented? In any case, what is he going to do about it? This organization made recommendations concerning old age pensions. When the Old Age Pensions Act was being discussed here last week, I did not see the smiling face of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) bob up and say: Mr. Speaker, before this act is passed I want to put on the record what Percy Bengough said on April 10, 1951, when he appeared with the executive of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada before the cabinet. There was nothing about that. Percy Bengough and the other members of the executive who signed the report were completely forgotten and ignored. There was present on that occasion: Percy Bengough, president; J. A. Whitebone, vice president from the maritimes; Claude Jodoin, vice president; William Jenoves, vice president; Carl E. Berg, vice president; Birt Showier, vice president; Gordon Cushing, general secretary treasurer.
The Minister of Justice made no mention of the proposals they made to the government. They were not speaking only for a few judges; they were not speaking for people who were already getting generous pensions, particularly when you compare them with the $480 that Percy Bengough will have to get along with, I suppose, when he is no longer able to carry on, and the amount upon which Angus Maclnnis will have to get along with when he is no longer able to carry on. Let us see what they proposed in regard to old age pensions. The proposals are listed as follows:
1.	That the means test be abolished.

2.	That all old age and blind pensions become the sole responsibility of the federal government.
3.	That the monthly pension payment be increased to $65 as a preliminary and interim measure while the machinery is being developed for the implementation of a full social security scheme.
4.	That the pensionable age be reduced for men to 65 and for women to 60.
5.	That suitable housing arrangements be undertaken for all recipients where such is needed.
I said I did not hear the Minister of Justice put in a plug for any of those proposals. But when he comes to take up the case of those who have, as I said, a pension which provides luxurious living in comparison with the pensions the aged people have, he quotes with approval the person whose submissions the government have ignored for the last fifteen or twenty years they have been in office.
Then let me turn to health insurance. Percy Bengough and the executive of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada had something to say about health insurance, but so far this session I have not heard the Minister of Justice supporting their claim. On page 5 of the submission they say:
Illness is still our greatest social and economic problem. More suffering is caused to individuals and families through sickness than from anything else. More financial troubles arise as a result of illness than from any other cause. Sickness frustrates production and will interfere with efforts to build up our defences more than all other factors combined. The time has long since passed when this problem should have been tackled with the will to solve it. Late as it is, immediate efforts should now be made.
I say the minister made no claims in regard to that. I could go through the whole of the submissions, all of them dealing with matters that vitally affect the people of this country, the people who are continually on the verge of poverty; and he has not raised his voice to help them.
I want to say a word about the salaries and the increases made.

This statement of mine is incorrect. The figures which I quoted represent cash income received by the farmers from farm operations. It does not include the farmer's income from Prairie Farm Assistance Act, from investments, or from any source other than farm income. Nor does it include the value of home consumed produce and inventories. In the table that was presented for farm cash income the figure shown for 1938 is 68-6. I mention that because this is the year before which the dominion bureau of statistics had no comparative data as regards net farm income. That was the point that the hon. member for Acadia was making. Now, our net farm income table starts at 1938, and in that context the index is shown as 100 as compared with this other index figure for farm cash income for 1938 at 68-6.
By 1950 this net farm income had gone up to 377-5. Thus the increase in net farm income after the payment of costs from 100 in 1938 to 377-5 in 1950 is even more favourable, much more favourable, to my argument than the increase in the farm cash income.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Yes, Liberal candidates, at least by implication. This is the sort of
Judges Act
charge that one would expect to hear as a rumour in the street, but not from a member of the house in a parliamentary debate. When the hon. member made it I must confess I was rather unprepared, and in my reply I said, as the fact was, that only a small percentage of such defeated candidates had been appointed during my own term of office. This matter of the appointment of proper candidates to the judiciary is so extremely important that I feel constrained now to lay before the house the cases-but of course I will not mention the names-of those defeated candidates who have been appointed since November 15, 1948.
To begin with, out of a total number of appointments of 68 there were only two former federal defeated candidates. When I say "former" I mean there were not any who had been defeated a reasonably short time before their appointment to the bench, but there were some who at some stage in their career had sustained defeat, two of them in federal elections and eight in provincial elections.
In a country like Canada where, in order to carry on our democratic form of government, we must have elections from time to time, I would think that it was not really a stain upon a man's character that he should have taken part in one of those elections, or even that he should have been defeated. But if it is a stain upon his character then I suggest that, if he has been defeated in that way, if he carries on as a respectable member of society and does his work well, it is a stain which he ultimately can hope to remove, and that after an interval it would be proper not to disqualify him on that ground alone as a potential candidate for the judiciary. But in the case of every one of these ten men who at some stage of their careers, in some cases eighteen to twenty years before, had been defeated candidates, I want to show one by one that the other qualifications which they possessed admirably fitted them for the position to which they were appointed, in spite of their being defeated candidates. I shall do that because I think it is important, for the confidence that the people of Canada should have in the judiciary of this country, that we put an end to this canard that the main qualifications for judges is that they should be defeated candidates.
The first of this group of ten is a man who was defeated after he had had a long and distinguished career in the House of Commons. I do not think that that sort of career disqualifies him for appointment to the bench because I have a rather good impression of

Judges Act
my fellow members of this House of Commons. I think that as a group they will compare quite favourably with any other similar number of Canadians that you will find anywhere in Canada; and that while we must take great care to see that the lawyer who is appointed to the bench has the necessary legal qualifications for the position, the fact that he has been a member of this house in my view-I may be wrong-rather tends to qualify than disqualify him for judicial appointment.
The second defeated candidate was a man whom I recommended for appointment to the county court bench. In relation to his appointment I think I received a larger number of recommendations from individual members of the bar, from businessmen, from organizations and from representatives of all political parties-except, as it happened, the Social Credit party-than I received for any other candidate. There is no doubt whatever about his eminent qualifications for the position.
The next one was a highly successful practitioner, a comfortably well off, if not wealthy, man, who did not apply for the position, nor was it applied for on his behalf by any of his political friends. We went to him and asked him if he would take the judicial position because we thought of all the men who were available or who could be persuaded to become available he was the most suitable candidate.
The fourth man was the acknowledged leader of the bar in the large city in which he lived. He had in the course of the decade preceding his appointment made earnings at the bar and in the community which made him a moderately wealthy man, and in relation to his earnings at the time that he was appointed he sustained a heavy financial sacrifice by going on the bench.
The next was a professor of civil procedure in the law school in one of our largest Canadian universities, a former batonnier of the bar of his province, a member of the commissioners on uniformity of legislation of the Canadian Bar Association, a member of the commission on the revision of the Criminal Code, and an author of two textbooks on law. Are we going to say that such a man should not be appointed to the bench because at one time in his life he had sustained the alleged disgrace of standing for election and being defeated, although in order to maintain our system of government we must have elections once in a while and we must have good candidates to run in them?
The next was a man who was outstanding in the criminal law, having been a crown attorney of one of the large judicial districts

in a large province, from 1921 to 1936, and had after that followed with a distinguished career as a defence lawyer at the criminal bar.
The next was a man who had been crown attorney for a period of five years, and was a distinguished pioneer resident of a northern part of the province from which he was appointed.
The next appointment was that of a man who, it is true, had been a defeated candidate once upon a time in his younger days, but redeemed himself by being successful in his subsequent elections, and had become attorney general of the province in which he was appointed.
The next one was a resident of one of the smaller provinces who had an excellent practice and was a thoroughly reliable practitioner, and whose defeat at the polls had taken place many years before he was appointed.
As to the last candidate, perhaps I should not include him because he was defeated at the polls in 1932 in Newfoundland, many years before Newfoundland became a province of Canada. But he redeemed that by going on to become what would correspond to the minister of justice in Canada and to * become lieutenant governor of that province; he was lieutenant governor before he was appointed to the bench.
These are all the actual appointments in relation to which this aspersion was cast yesterday by the hon. member for Macleod. As I have known him for many years as a very fair gentleman, I would hope that when he has this explanation he will see fit to withdraw the charge he made.

Before the clause is carried, I should like to say that I am in favour of this legislation because I want to see everybody happy, and a judge who is unhappy does not give good judgments. It is in the interests of the litigants as well as of the bench that the judges should live a comfortable life and enjoy independent means.
I will take this opportunity to make another remark that has been in my mind for a long time. Judges expect to enjoy the respect of everybody, which is natural. They will do so in so far as they stop using unpalatable language with regard to judges of other jurisdiction. I have never heard anybody complain so bitterly about judges as judges themselves. I hope they will be tolerant and will not take the attitude of being depositories

of the revealed truth. There is too much of that, and it is impossible to argue with them.
Very often some of them do not take the trouble to study a case upon its merits. They follow the jurisprudence and render judgments just the same as a butcher makes sausages. Of course there are exceptions, and worthy exceptions, but the publication of compendiums of jurisprudence has a particularly bad effect upon the quality of the judgments rendered by some judges. Very often les juges, or summaries of judgments or dissenting opinions, are not supposed to render absolutely the various shades of thought that the judges have taken so much trouble to try to make understood by those who listen to them or read their judgments. I do not say that to show any disrespect for the bench itself. I understand that the position of judges is very difficult because they act with litigants as the United Nations does with belligerents. They try to appease them as much as they can.
Let me tell you how I used to practice in my own law office years ago. I had a large office with my desk in the middle and there were two rows of chairs on each side. Very often both parties came to my office for a settlement. At first they would abuse each other in the most vociferous language. I did not listen to them. It was too noisy, and I thought of something else. When there was a lull I used to tell them: Gentlemen, now that you have reached an agreement, what will you do? They would say: We have not reached any agreement; we are not going to reach any agreement with that fellow across your desk. Then I would say: "Keep quiet, please", and they would start again. This time it was not so long, and after a few minutes they were ready to come to an amicable settlement. Some judges practice that way, and it is the best way instead of following the practice of Philadelphia lawyers.
I am glad this legislation has been brought before the House of Commons, for the reasons I have given.

I should like to comment first of all on subsection 4. I am very glad to see this subsection in the bill. Having advocated such an amendment to the act since I came into the house in 1945,' and having pressed the minister and his predecessors on the subject both in the house and in correspondence, I wish to express my gratification that this amendment is now being made. I consider that a great injustice was done in 1944 that, when the right of election was extended to

the judges to divide their annuities with their widows if their wives survived them, the same privilege was not extended to judges who happened to have retired prior to August 15, 1944. That shortcoming is now being corrected by this subsection, and I for one wish to express my gratification on finding it in the bill.
There is one other matter on which I should like to make brief comment with reference to the option now given to judges either to retain their annuity for themselves exclusively or to make the other choice of dividing it with their widows should their wives survive them. The exercise of the option under present circumstances is irrevocable. But in a case where a judge has made his election in favour of dividing his annuity with his widow, if he happens to survive his wife he receives only two-thirds of the annuity. By reason of the fact that he guessed wrong as to whether his wife might or might not survive him, he is deprived thereby of one-third of the pension he would otherwise receive. I do not think that is fair. If a judge is married at the time he exercises his option, exercises it in favour of his wife, and then his wife predeceases him, it seems to me only fair that he should be entitled to the full pension, and that he should not be penalized to the extent of one-third of his annuity because his wife has predeceased him.
It strikes me that the crown is obliging the judge under those circumstances to wager on his wife surviving him. It is not fair, and in the treatment of our judges I do not think we need to resort to a basis like that. I urge on the minister that, where a married judge has exercised his option in favour of his wife, and then his wife predeceases him, he should be entitled to his full annuity without deduction because of the fact that he guessed wrong as to whether or not his wife would survive him.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INCREASE IN SALARIES AND NUMBERS OF JUDGES
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot agree with my hon. friend. The judge has not guessed wrong at all. He is getting full actuarial value for the election which he made. The situation is this. The judge has a certain pension. In the interests of protecting his wife he has been given the privilege of dividing it into three parts and making one of those parts payable to his wife for her life.

If she survives him, and the wives survive the husbands in more cases than vice versa. The intention of the government was to enable the judge to dispose of his pension in a way in which the judge and

his wife would be protected during the lifetime of both of them, and the survivor would be protected for his or her lifetime. We wanted to do that at no cost, if possible, to the taxpayer because the taxpayer is entitled to some consideration in this matter. The hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough says that these very deserving county court judges should have a much larger increase than they are getting. Perhaps there may be something to his argument, but some consideration also has to be paid to the people who are paying the bill.
When the judge elects to divide his pension in that way he is in effect buying an annuity for his wife equal to one-third of his own pension and payable for her life, whether she survives him or not. He is getting actuarial value for that. He cannot have his cake and eat it too. He cannot get that protection, which any insurance man will tell my hon. friend can only be attained by paying a premium of so much money value, and at the same time say that after the risk has not turned out in the way he anticipated when he paid his premium he would like to get his money back. On that basis, if I insure my house for three years and it does not burn down in that period I could go back to the insurance company and say that since it certainly had not lost anything in carrying the fire risk on my house it should give me back my premium. By a more intelligent arrangement of the judge's pension for the benefit of himself and his wife we planned to guard against widows of judges being left destitute and we planned to do this at the lowest possible cost to the taxpayer. The amount of money we pay the widows of judges under this arrangement is more than we save through the judge getting only two-thirds of his pension where his wife predeceases him. It is true that the difference is not a large sum of money, but it is something. So I do not think if is at all fair to say the judge gets no value for his money, and the proof of that is in the fact that the great majority of judges have very wisely, I think, seen fit to make this election.

To provide for the defence forces of the navy, army and air services and defence research and development, and to authorize total commitments for this purpose of $3,831,270,000 including authority notwithstanding section 29 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, to make commitments for the current year of $1,924,170,835 and commitments against future years of $1,907,099,165 against which commitments it is estimated that actual expenditures in 1951-52 will not exceed $1,595,050,000 of which $183,050,000 will he provided from section 3 of the Defence Appropriation Act 1950 as supplemented by item 246, $1,412,000,000.

When the committee rose to report progress last night, we were considering the detail dealing with the acquisition

and construction of buildings. I was questioning the amount in this item, namely, $3,350,000. I understood that $350,000 would be spent on civil defence and the balance, namely, $3 million was to be spent on acquiring land, preparing plans and starting on the construction of a new defence headquarters here in the city of Ottawa. I was wondering whether there was any real necessity for such construction to start this year, in view of the fact that the present headquarters now occupied by national defence was built towards the end of the last war. From all outward appearances, it seems to be in first-class condition.
We have been told that there is a considerable shortage of steel across the country, and ther? is not a plentiful supply of other building materials. There is a great demand for private homes as well as other government buildings. In fact, buildings are required in this department, such as barracks, homes for the soldiers, drillhalls, armouries, airfields and so forth. I wondered whether we were really justified in spending this large sum of money for this particular purpose. I was not entirely satisfied with the answer which was given by the minister, and I should like to know if he has anything to say in amplification of the brief remarks he made last night? When was the present building now occupied by the headquarters of the three services constructed, and what was the cost of it?

I think it is agreed by all hon. members that some day the Department of National Defence should move away from Cartier square. That being so, the question arises as to whether it is not wise on our part to acquire the land on which to build the future national defence headquarters, and to begin work on the plans. That is all that is contemplated this year, and that has not yet been decided upon. I would point out that it is desirable that we should acquire the site, not only for the purpose of having the site but for the purpose of being able to plan now other arrangements related to it, such as transportation and communication facilities as well as other accommodations.
Then there is a question of the adequacy of the present accommodation compared to what we had during the war. On Cartier square we have at present three buildings now known as A, B and C. They provide a floor space of 536,000 square feet. At the peak of the war we were using in Ottawa an additional 1,903,646 square feet, or a total of 2,439,646 square feet. At the present time we have the buildings A, B and C on Cartier square providing 536,000 square feet,
Supply-National Defence and in addition we have in the district of Ottawa approximately another 320,000 square feet. At the present time, therefore, we have approximately 850,000 square feet, or about one-third of what we had at the peak of the war.
Can the minister say what it cost to erect the buildings now occupied?

Yes. Building A, which is the old naval service headquarters, cost $830,350.38; building C, which is the old army annex, cost $1,007,125; and building B, which is the old R.C.A.F. building on Lisgar street, cost $527,052.34. This totals $2,364,527.72.

No; under the plans for the federal district for Ottawa, it is intended that they would be removed. My recollection is that one or two large public buildings would be located there. '
To all intents and purposes we are going to say goodbye to this $2 million?
Undoubtedly there would be some salvage through the crown assets disposal corporation. I cannot give an estimate of what we would get.
The minister would not get very much for that. When was this building completed? Was it in 1944?
These buildings were completed at three different periods, but I think they were all completed by 1943.
This item of $3 million is purely for the acquisition of land?
And the preparation of plans.
Could the minister say how much land is envisaged?

We have not settled that, but it would be a very considerable area. It would, of course, depend on the location. If it were some distance from the centre of Ottawa it would be necessary to provide services and other accommodations.

No.

The minister has said it is desirable to move the present headquarters from its location. Is that because of the necessity of fitting in with the national plan for Ottawa or what is the reason?

Supply-National Defence

The building itself is a temporary wartime building and will not last forever. It has to be replaced at some future date. It is a good wartime building and it is in good condition, provided it is well maintained; and the maintenance costs are quite high. I think there was a fairly clear understanding that when Cartier square was used for that purpose it would be released at some date; and the federal district plan provides for the location of defence headquarters somewhere else.

Have we the minister's assurance that no construction will be started on this new building until such a future time as materials which are needed for housing and other urgently needed buildings are again in free supply?

I can give the assurance that the Minister of Defence Production will watch that situation carefully, and that I certainly do not believe that the building will be started this year except for the acquisition of land, the commencement of plans, and conceivably the planning and preliminary work, also some services that it might be convenient to do in conjunction with some other operations might begin this year; but no construction.
Then 'I take it that no construction will be started until building materials are again in free supply. Is that correct?

That will have to be con->
sidered by the Minister of Defence Production having regard to all the considerations and the various priorities involved. But I cannot conceive of that building being started this year.

Had the estimates been prepared in a different way, Mr. Chairman, and if this subitem were an item by itself, one would be in a position to move a reduction in this estimate by the amount which is now proposed to be spent on these headquarters, if one felt that it was an unnecessary expenditure. I am not convinced yet as to the necessity for this building and for this expenditure of money. I recall the fact that earlier this year, when speaking on his estimates-and this is to be found at page 2805 of Hansard-the minister assured this committee that he was going to observe the utmost in the way of economy in the expenditure of this large sum of money which he has at his disposal. As reported at the same page he went on to say:
... we will see to it that the best possible use is made of this money.
Owing to the way in which these estimates are presented, it would not be possible to

move a reduction at this stage without affecting the whole item which embraces many other details. As we go on with the examination of these estimates, it may be that we shall find other items with the necessity for which we are not impressed. While I say this item may therefore be carried, I do so with the reservation that when we consider the total we may have the right to move a reduction of the amount shown here, one which appears at the moment to be an extravagant and unnecessary expenditure at the present time. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, if you will accept the "carried" as it will be given now as meaning that we have ceased debating on this subitem, well and good; but I reserve the right to move a reduction, with particular reference to this construction, when we come to the end of the item.

It seems to me that it would be in good condition for another ten years anyway. The facilities we have at the present time handled forces amounting to nearly one million men and women during the last war. It therefore seems to me that it must have the physical capacity to handle our needs for the present and for the foreseeable future. Desirable though it might be to have a nice new building started and completed soon, again the money that pays for that building must come out of the taxpayers' pockets. If a building of this kind requires an outlay of $3 million just for land and plans, I would say that by the time it is completed it will cost many millions of dollars that again must come out of the taxpayers' pockets.
I see no justification at all for starting on a project of this kind at this time when taxes are high, when the cost of living is high and when people are being taxed heavily. I can see no justification for this expenditure at all. I would request the minister to explain why a building that was completed at the end of the last war, that seems to be in first-class shape, that handled personnel of almost one million men and women in the armed forces in the last war, would not be adequate for a number of years, and why it is necessary to start on a new building at the present time.

As I understand it, we are dealing with repairs and upkeep of buildings. Earlier in the session I directed a question to the minister regarding the central ordnance depot No. 27 at London, Ontario. A couple of days later he replied saying that increased security precautions were being taken. All this came about in response to the disastrous fire here in Ottawa, where large quantities of military stores were lost.
In the very early hours of Tuesday morning I took the opportunity to go down to the central ordnance depot. It is in my riding. I went down there to see what conditions were like and I want to say to the minister that the guards were on duty. They were carrying out their work apparently very efficiently, and I could attach no fault whatever to the men and the personnel who were engaged in that work. What I want to say is this. I still do not believe that sufficient security precautions are being taken. We have an investment there of $60 million, spread over an area of some thirty-five or forty acres. They have a self-contained fire fighting equipment and force, but it is not on duty at night. In view of the increasing seriousness of the world situation, it would seem to me that greater precautions should and must be taken not only at London but in all the military installations of one kind and another.	1
It is pretty obvious that sabotage is abroad, and that with the increasing world tension it may increase. We could become very weak militarily if sabotage should crop up in every

Supply-National Defence city that has military equipment of one kind or another in stores. I am just mentioning the central ordnance as an example.
The security officer was training two new men when I arrived there. I could find no fault at all with them in any way, but I do not think we have taken the necessary precautions.

I am very glad the hon.
member brought this up. Naturally we are very conscious of it. The security guards on duty at night are there not only to guard against fire but to give first assistance in the putting out of a fire. Imperial war graves commission-
Canada's share of maintenance of war graves of world war II, $424,227.

Has it been brought to the minister's attention that the graves of the Polish soldiers who fell in Europe in the last war and who were serving so gallantly with the first Canadian army are not being maintained and kept in the same condition as the graves of the Canadian soldiers, the point being I believe that Canada is responsible for a certain amount of money for the maintenance of the graves of Canadian soldiers. Now, suppose there were Norwegian soldiers who had been fighting with us or Norwegian airmen, as there were: the Kingdom of Norway would be responsible for the maintenance of those graves. But so far as the Polish soldiers are concerned, we have a situation where the present government of Poland does not regard the Poles who were fighting in a Polish division with the Canadian army as being patriots of Poland. I understand that today the government of Poland is providing no contribution toward the maintenance of the graves of any Polish soldiers. That may be the reason why these graves are neglected, as I understand they are, at the present time. Therefore, in view of the great contribution which the Polish division made to the cause for which Canada was fighting and the fact that that Polish division was part of the Canadian army, will the government give consideration either to increasing its contribution or seeing that these graves are properly marked and properly maintained?

We will be very glad indeed to give that consideration. Of course the hon.

member knows that we are partners in the imperial war graves commission, and even if we desired to do so we would have to consult them; but I will be glad to look into it.
Because they were fighting with us.

This is a very important item. Can the minister give the committee this assurance, that the grave of any man who fought at any time with the allies, irrespective of origin or place of birth, and made the ' supreme sacrifice, will be properly marked and looked after? Will the minister give me assurance that everything in his power will be done along that line?

In so far as they are veterans who served with Canadian forces, that is being done. In so far as they are veterans who served alongside the Canadian forces, we will have to look into the case, and we shall be glad to do so.
If they fought for the same cause does the minister not think that the taxpayer would be glad to see that their graves are properly looked after?
There are a great many different cases. For example, Italians fought side by side with us, and I could mention others. They would have to be investigated.
I do not care what the nationality is.
How are the amounts apportioned among the different nations of the imperial war graves commission?
It is related to the number of graves. Canada's graves number 43,391, or 7-8 per cent of the total, and our contribution to the fund is made on that basis. Those are ours in the great war of 1914-18.
In other words we look after our own graves.
Yes.

I should like to ask a question which was brought to the attention of the house last year and I did not hear how the matter was finally resolved. The suggestion was that permanent headstones in the cemeteries in Europe did not bear the regimental insignia, the names of the regiments of the soldiers who lost their lives. I was in one of the cemeteries myself, where the permanent headstones gave the name, the number and rank, and then just the notation, "Canadian Corps of Infantry" or "Canadian Artillery". They did not have the regimental names or crests. This point was raised last year, but I have not heard how it was resolved.

I strongly urge the minister that if the regimental insignia and regimental names are not on permanent headstones, steps should be taken to see that they are put on.

About two years ago, when
this matter was first brought to my attention,
I looked into it at once. The government decided that in respect of all Canadians killed in the second world war the headstones should bear the names of their regiments or corps and dates of death, in addition to ranks, regimental numbers and the names of the deceased. It was also decided that in the case of soldiers whose origin was known to be French the headstones would be in that language, and also that the signs at cemeteries and the direction signs leading to cemeteries would be in both languages, as well as the language of the country in which the cemetery was located.

And that is being done
now-all headstones are being altered?

Yes. In the case of some
which were erected before this was brought to my attention, we shall replace or change these when we have completed the rest.

Would the minister explain
the policy being followed in so far as the graves of soldiers who fall in Korea are concerned. It may be that the imperial war graves commission has not yet set up an organization in the Far East. While it is practical for people to visit graves of relatives who have fallen in Europe, it is an entirely different matter, and probably will be for many years, for people to visit the graves of men who fell in Korea. Would the government give consideration to bringing those bodies back to Canada, because I see the greatest difficulty for visitors wishing to go to Korea.

Consideration has been
given to that matter, but no decision has been reached. Naturally we would want to co-operate with our sister nations in the commonwealth, as we have so far agreed on our policy with respect to the disposition of bodies of service personnel who have been killed. I appreciate the difficulty to which the hon. member refers, and consideration will be given to the final disposition.

I do not wish to take up time
of the committee, except to say that I entirely disagree with both the minister and the hon. member for Nanaimo.
I have not made any decision.

I think it is a great mistake,
as the Americans have done, to bring great numbers of soldiers back home for burial in their own land. I am sure if the soldiers
Supply-National Defence themselves could have been consulted they would have wanted to rest where they were. As for the parents being able to get to Europe and to other places, well, I do not suppose that there is one parent in five or six hundred who will see those graves, whether they are in Europe, Korea or wherever they may be. For my part I hope the minister will not give too serious consideration to the matter.

Subitem agreed to.

increase? Is it accounted for by the increase in the number of people in the dockyards, or just what is the reason for this considerable increase?

This increase is partly
explained by the increased salaries and pay of civilian workers, and in part by increased activities of the navy. The numbers are to be increased from 6,331 to 7,121, an increase of 790. How many of those 7,121
are employed in dockyards?

At Halifax there are 2,459
and at Esquimalt 1,987.

What are these civilian
allowances? Why is the item here at all?

Subitem agreed to.
Pay and allowances, $30,879,387.
Would the minister say how recruiting is progressing so far as the navy is concerned toward the objective that was set?

The present strength of the navy as at June 25, 1951-and of course it is an estimate in respect of the month of June-is officers, 1,593, and men, 10,115, a total of 11,708. Recruiting for the navy over
4776	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence the past six months has been as follows: January, 288; February, 476; March, 591; April, 421; May, 249; and June, up to the 25th, 383: a total of 2,508. It is meeting the planned requirements.

I have a question to ask on that point which I think will be of general interest. When are they going to start to recruit a women's division for the navy as has already been undertaken for the army and the air force?

We shall be recruiting women for the naval reserve at a very early date. The date has not yet been fixed, but I would expect it would be some time during the summer. To organize and assist in that work we will be calling up a limited number of women's naval reserve officers for full time service. It is not the present intention to recruit women for the regular navy.

Has any consideration been given to the establishment of an allowance for a dependent mother, or dependent mother and father? There is an allowance for the wife and children. There are many cases- and I have written about some of them myself-where the dependent is either the mother, or the mother and father. It applies to all services. Has the department given any consideration to that matter?

In answer to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, consideration has been given to the matter. It has been raised by him and a great number of other members. However, as I explained before-and I will be glad to give the hon. member the reference to the explanation-in planning increased pay rates on a unified basis for all three services in 1946 an effort was made to approximate the scales of pay and allowances of officers and men of the armed services to those which men doing equivalent work, and of equivalent seniority, would get in the eight leading industries of Canada. At that time a very extensive study was made as a consequence of which the pay rates were established. It was decided at that time not to make any allowance in respect of mothers and other relatives other than the wife and children. So far it has been the view of the services, I may say, and of the government, that we should adhere to that policy. Whether or not we could do it if the armed forces continue to grow at the rate they are, and if our undertakings and activities extend further, remains to be seen, but the matter is being constantly considered.

I should like to follow that up. While the situation creates considerable hardship where the enlisted person maintains a home, there is another angle which is much worse. There is something coming home


while the boy is living; there is an assignment of pay. But if he dies on service then the dependents are in a rather awkward position to go to the Department of Veterans Affairs and claim a pension of any kind. It is a rather serious problem, and a large number of service personnel are affected when you consider the three services. I am glad the minister is considering it, and I hope he will come to a final conclusion soon.
The minister gave the number of officers and men in the navy as at June 25. I should like to ask how many officers and men it is estimated that the amount of $30,879,387 will cover.
At the present time 13,440.
In other words, this $30 million odd will pay for-
And I take it that is the number you expect to recruit by the end of the year?
Yes. At the current rate we will do better than that, and if so we will find the money for them from some other source or ask for a supplementary if necessary.

The minister said that women's naval reserve officers might be called up later. Has he any intention of taking married women? There are a number who were in before and they would like to get back into active service again.
Certainly we will give preference to single women, and whether or not we take on married women will depend on the number of single women who offer their services.
What would happen if a married woman applied now?
We would put her on a list.
You would put her on a list?
Yes.
There are some who wish to join. I know some of them, and they would make good officers now just as they did in the last war.

Is there any portion of this item contained in the item of $329 million referred to yesterday, and which is to be found on page 275? I do not know whether the minister would like us to ask in each case if any proportion of the particular amount is carried over into the $329 million, or whether when we come to that amount under the final item the minister will be prepared to present a table showing how that sum is arrived at.

I can give the basis of it when we come to it or now, but there will not be any list. There is no list of items because it is arrived at by examination of the total for the navy, army, air force and defence research. In arriving at that estimate we make full provision for pay and allowances, food, clothing, and.so on, for the number of men we plan to take on at the times we plan to take them on.
The minister was able to give a fairly definite amount last evening of $1,900,000.
That is the only specific item.
That is the only one in which you can give a definite amount?
Yes.
All the rest is just an approximate estimate?
That is right.
So it is no use asking whether any proportion of this can be saved. The minister will simply say he hopes to save something.
That is right; not on pay and allowances, but on construction.
You may save something on that?
Yes. I can give the items for the navy, army, air force and defence research.
Perhaps it would be better to give them at the end.

If I have understood the minister correctly his statement seems to flatly contradict what I understood him to say last night when we were talking about the item of $3 million for headquarters. At that time I understood him to say he was able to assure us that of this figure of $329 million on page 275, $1,900,000 represented the headquarters building.
Yes.

Then I cannot square that with what the minister just said, that we cannot get similar figures in respect of each of the items, some of which run into tens of millions of dollars. He now says all that is done is to take what I understand to be a percentage figure at the end;
Supply-National Defence in other words that the $329 million does not mean what I at any rate thought it meant last night, that it is just a percentage calculation.

I am sorry the hon. member misunderstood me. That probably arose from the fact that in the case of departmental administration we are dealing with a branch of the department which is relatively static and similar to that of another government department. It is not expanding like the armed forces; it is not dealing with large amounts for construction, except for this single item. In that case, as I say, $1,900,000 was considered very unlikely to be spent in 1951-52.
In the case of the navy, army and air force, however, we have found that if we estimate in detail for a program of $1,900 million, as we do, covering literally hundreds of thousands of projects, we are not going to be able to complete all of them; and from our experience we have found that in1 the case of the navy, approximately 15 per cent will not be spent. In the case of the air force because of the nature of the equipment, particularly aircraft, the uncertainties involved in the procurement of material from the United States and construction problems, the factor is 221 per cent, while in the case of the army it is 15 per cent, If we did not do it in this wiay we would be faced with two alternatives, either of which would be much less satisfactory than the present arrangement. If we put in detailed estimates which were fixed covering the total program of $1,900 million, from our experience we would not be able to spend more than $1,500 million or some figure of that magnitude, and therefore we would have an unexpended surplus of from $300 to $400 million in respect of national defence. We would be asking parliament for more money than we knew we could spend. If on the other hand we put in for the cash we knew we could spend, say $1,500 million to give the example, and no more, the same principle would still apply and because of the uncertainties due to delivery of equipment that is still in the process of development, construction and other uncertainties, we would spend only $1,200 million, and that at a time when we are increasing the armed forces at the present rate.
Hon. members will recall that when I appeared before them at this time last year I was seeking $425 million. The amount we are likely to spend this year through all sources is about $1,780 million, four times as much. That rate of increase is far greater than we experienced at any time during the second world war. Indeed today we are spending on defence more than we did during either the first or second year of the second

Supply-National Defence world war. The same situation exists in the United States. They have a cash appropriation for a much larger sum than they can spend, but they can carry it over from year to year. This arrangement was worked out by the Department of Finance to give the utmost possible control over the program and at the same time provide for flexibility so we might spend as much as possible to do the most we can in each fiscal year.

Supply-National Defence supplies, $185,000; ammunition and bombs, $16,240,999; barracks, camp, hospital and miscellaneous stores, $5,788,560.
I obtained a statement which I might give to hon. members-it is rather interesting-on the extent of operations of some of the ships in Korean waters.
