What is the amount in that item by which the figure exceeds the actual amount that it is expected will be spent?
It is 15 per cent over-all of the whole naval program.

No, no. In the case of an earlier item we dealt with, the minister was able to tell us what amount he did not expect to spend. In dollars and cents what is the amount of this $60,189,708 that it is not expected will be spent this year?

As I explained a few minutes ago, Mr. Chairman, the amount that is not expected to be spent, out of the total program for the navy of $277,754,980, is $41,663,247 or 15 per cent. It is spread over the whole naval program.
The minister has indicated that he has this information in regard to other Items. Has he no more definite information in this case?

That is not the way it is arrived at. We have that information for the item I mentioned. But I told hon. members last night that I would give the basis in respect of the navy, the army, the air force and defence research.
Is any change in design of uniform contemplated?

No; certainly no major
change. I have not had one submitted to me.
I know of none.
From what the minister has said, I understood that this item covered the commissioning of new ships.
No.
I thought the minister said that.
No. There was a phrase that may have given that impression; it was stores required in connection with the commissioning of new ships.

Subitem agreed to.
Acquisition and construction of buildings and works, including acquisition of land, $24,147,000.

I want to come back to the question we have had up several times, and I am doing it in connection with acquisition and construction of buildings because, as we go through the three services, there are some $292 million, if my addition is correct, for this purpose. Incidentally, I want to point out that what is happening now is illustrating and underlining the fact that we could do this job so much better if we had been able to have a workmanlike committee instead of the committee of the whole house; but I just mention that in passing.
I want to come back again to last evening, and to point out that the acquisition and construction of buildings and works, so far as I can see, is exactly the kind of thing that is done by the Department of Public Works. Again, I thought that last evening we were clear that the Department of National Defence was following the same practice. But it now appears that it was only with respect to the headquarters that that illustration was given.
I want to point out where this leaves the ordinary member of parliament. We have this $292 million which we authorize. We have no details of any of the buildings or of the land which is being acquired. We have to take the whole thing on trust. There is nothing which will enable us afterwards to test the efficiency of what is done, because we have no figures now except this general, over-all figure. What I want to ask the minister is this. Let us leave out the procurement of war materials as something which may perhaps have a special feature of its own which prevents us from applying to it ordinary business considerations. But in the case of the acquisition and construction of buildings, why may we not have the same details as we get in the case of public works?
I admit that this over-all percentage is an easy way out; it is a comfortable way to work. I am sure it probably lessens the amount of work. But as the hon. member for Calgary East said last night, it simply means that to say that parliament has any supervision over this is just to take part in a solemn farce. With the amount of information that we are able to get in this way, we have no real supervision.

Mr. Chairman, I think I have already explained the position with regard to this matter. The situation is this. We have a construction program, which we should like to see completed this year, of $300 million. I think it is more than the hon. gentleman mentions. We have a list of projects. We are endeavouring to proceed with those projects as rapidly as we can. We do that through the instrumentality of the Department of Defence Production, Defence Construction Limited and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We draw plans, issue specifications, process them, let them to tenders; and in order to do that we also have to acquire the land where we have not got it. We cannot tell at this time what proportion of that great program will be completed. We know that we are not even going to begin on some of it this year because of lack of materials, lack of labour, or because other things on which construction is dependent have not yet happened. The situation is quite different from that in the case of the Department of Public Works which, I understand, processes each case before it is put in the estimates, so that it snows within a very small factor exactly what it is going to do in respect of each fiscal year. We cannot know that. We put in the full list of the program we have planned, with the possibility of proceeding this year in some, not proceeding this year in others, never proceeding in some because we change our minds upon further consideration. If all this was ditched now we would lead to a state of confusion which I think would be rather serious. We would have all kinds of representations made by very responsible people that we should proceed with this, that and the other thing, and hon. members know what that involves in the way of activity. But we would also disclose our hand as to the time of proceeding with a great number of things such as additional magazines, ancillary buildings, seaward defences and the like. Frankly I do not think it is practicable to give the details in the estimates. I do not think it would be in the interest of economy and good business practice-I am not talking security at all- to give details of the construction program because it is so likely to change during the year.

Can the minister tell us
whether the cost of the two service colleges, or part of the cost, is covered under this item?

There is a provision here for an addition at Royal Roads, but that has not
Supply-National Defence been approved yet by the treasury board. It may be a matter that we shall have to delay until another year.

I should like to find out from the minister the actual cost of the service colleges, because on May 10 the minister answered a question of mine in which I asked for a service college in Quebec, and opposed it by saying that it would cost too much. I should like to know how much these service colleges cost.
I will get the information for the hon. member.
When may I expect it? Under which item?
It does not come under this item, but I will give it to the hon. member either before we rise at six o'clock or at eight o'clock.

While I am on my feet I would like to advocate the opening of a service college for French-speaking Canadians, because as I pointed out earlier, we have very few senior officers of the French language and very few at the headquarters of our three defence services. I think something should be done about it. I am not pointing it out just to raise a racial cry or anything of that kind; I want to make sure that French-speaking Canadians get the same opportunity as other Canadians. We are not asking for any more than anybody else. We are not asking that the minister or the department or headquarters appoint officers who are not qualified. All we want is equality of opportunity. If we ask that an officer be promoted and they tell us that he is not qualified I would be the first one to say, do not appoint him. But I would also like to be sure that an officer of the French language gets the opportunity to qualify himself.
I think the department is making a grave mistake, and that is why I should like to know how much these service colleges cost, because out of a budget of over $1,500,000,000 I am pretty sure that an effort could be made in that way. It would help recruiting; it would help national unity in Canada, and it would also be a great uplift for young Canadians of the French language who enlist in the service today.
During the debate the other day the minister said that at the present time 25 per cent of the cadets are French-speaking. Well, on April 9, in a return from his department, I received the following figures-

Supply-National Defence
I just want to press my point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I know, but the hon. member must be in order when he presses his point.

I am advocating a defence college, and I am bringing out the arguments in favour of building such a defence college. I am asking the department to make certain expenditures. I just want to point out the necessity for it. I intend to be very brief. I just want to point out that the minister said that 25 per cent of the cadets were of French origin. According to the return I received on April 9, only 51 out of 509 were French-speaking Canadians. That is only 10 per cent instead of 25 per cent. Will the minister tell me now which of the two figures is right? Is it 10 per cent, according to the return I received on April 9, or 25 per cent, which is the figure that he used in his speech on May 10?

I will have to look at the return. The figures on the cost of Royal Roads, 1951-52, are $666,369 and Royal Military College $887,000. These are the estimates for the current year.
Answering the hon. member's suggestion, I do not rule out the possibility of there being a college in Quebec at some future time. I would hope that if there were it would be for English-speaking as well as for Frenchspeaking cadets. Our policy in the two colleges at Royal Roads and R.M.C. has been to make them colleges in which there is equality of leadership for Canadians of all origins and in the three services. We have been definitely of the view that it is very much better for English-speaking boys at these colleges to mix with French-speaking boys. We have made a special point of teaching French in the colleges. They have French conversational classes.
It seems to us that that is a good approach to the problem of national unity. However, I do not exclude the possibility of having' a college in Quebec either for French-speaking boys or for both. In the event of war I would think it would certainly be necessary, and the expense, whatever it might be, would be justified.
The hon. member would be interested to know that we are opening very shortly at the Royal Canadian Reserve division, H.M.C.S. Montcalm, a course for French-speaking entrants to the Royal Canadian Navy which will accustom them in their own environment to the ways of the navy, and also give them the opportunity to learn the technical terms and all those things which must necessarily be in one language.
We also hope to see established at Laval university a course in military science, where
[The Chairman.]
a special certificate will be given. We have been discussing that arrangement with the university and the archbishop. So that we are fully alive to the desirability of achieving the aim the hon. member has in mind, but we are not convinced that the method he suggests is necessarily the best one at the present time.
Since the matter has been raised, I should like to say in the most emphatic way possible that the proportionate number of Frenchspeaking officers in the three armed forces, of the rank of major and above, is just about the same as the proportion of Englishspeaking officers of the rank of major and above, in relation to the number of officers of the rank of captain and below. Also I can assure the hon. member that I have made a careful examination of the various categories of officers and I have found that, by and large, French-speaking officers receive promotion at a lower age and with less service than English-speaking officers, indicating that if there is any preference it is in their favour.

I would not want the minister to think that we are asking for preferential treatment. All we ask is equality of opportunity. The minister has said that there are just as many French-speaking of the rank of major, captain and so on, proportionately, as there are English-speaking. On the 15th of this month, out of 83 officers chosen to follow a staff course, there were only 3 French-speaking. Either that is discrimination or it shows that the minister does not think that French-Canadians should qualify.

It is not discrimination at all. The fact is that there are not as many Frenchspeaking officers, officers whose mother-tongue is French, as there should be, in proportion to the population. That is an unfortunate situation. But this is not due to any policy of the department. It is due to the fact that during the years between the wars it would seem that a career in the armed forces was not greatly attractive to French-speaking Canadians.
Since the war that situation has been entirely different. We are now getting a very good proportion of officers of French-speaking origin. The gap lies in the officers who might have joined between wars, but did not.

I am sure the minister does not expect to fill that gap if he keeps a percentage of 10 per cent of French-speaking officers in service colleges. I am not arguing for any preference or for any special treatment. We want only equality of opportunity. I know that, for the young officer who is not familiar with English, it is difficult for him to follow a course in artillery, or something of that

kind. He must go through all sorts of specialized courses just to learn basic English. You may be sure that is the main barrier in the enlistment of young French-speaking Canadians.
The department is making a terrific mistake in failing to see that point. I would be the last person in Canada to ask for the appointment of unqualified officers who would be in charge of the lives of other soldiers. However, I would ask that the department make an intelligent effort along these lines. I believe the establishment of a French-speaking service college, where the boys would have exactly the same training as they would receive in an English-speaking service college would bring satisfactory results.
The minister said the other day that the Royal 22nd Regiment, a French-speaking regiment, is equal to any other, and that others are equal to it. For myself I am ljot satisfied as to the real intentions of the department and of the minister when, only a week ago, out of 83 chosen to take a staff course, only 3 were French-speaking.

This is so important that I
think it must not be misunderstood. The proportion of three to eighty-three should be made in relation to the number of officers trying the entrance exam or to the total number of English and French-speaking officers in the armed forces. As I have said we are anxious to get the largest possible number of French-speaking officers. Far from there being any discrimination against them, as I have pointed out, the figures on promotions indicate that the balance is in their favour. French is regarded by me, by the chiefs of staff and by the department as a positive military asset, as indeed it is; and in every way, shape and form we possibly can we are doing our utmost not only to give equality but to make the best possible armed forces we can in Canada. For that we need a proper proportion of French-speaking Canadians.

Supply-National Defence
Can the minister say where the major amounts are being spent, and what lands are being acquired? Will he give us some details of this sum?

There are very big developments to complete the permanent barracks at the seaward defence base at Halifax. Then at Dartmouth there is a new barracks block, control tower and heating plant. On the west coast at Kamloops there are additional magazine facilities. At Montreal there is a central storage depot, and at Cornwallis a new building for recreation. Then there is additional construction in connection with the Dartmouth armament depot. At Esquimau there is a new barracks block, and there are a number of other smaller items. Included in the item are fifty-six married quarters units, and a large payment of $8,390,000 to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for married quarters that they are building for the navy. In Newfoundland we are beginning a new magazine. I mentioned the addition at Royal Roads, and at Regina there is a new reserve building. Included in this total is an amount of $500,000 for acquisition of real property. The rest is for construction.
Is there anything at William Head?
No.
Is that development under the navy?

We have it under a different name. It is acquisition of land. $100,000 is provided this year for the new magazine there and the cost of the land is included in the $500,000 item that I mentioned. That has not yet been established.

I want to add one word before this item carries. I want to reiterate what I said before, that we are put in the position of virtually issuing a blank cheque for something like $300 million in respect to these acquisitions. By reason of the method which the government has seen fit to adopt it has really been made impossible for us to have an intelligent interest in this matter. I think perhaps public opinion is becoming aroused, and it may be that public opinion will be of more interest to the government than it was a week ago.

I do not know whether this is the right item, but the Department of National Defence has expropriated a considerable amount of land in two small townships in my constituency. I should like to

If they come under the Municipal Grants Act then of course they would have the advantage of that act.

Major procurement of equipment, $110,954,383.
I do not think we can carry an item for $110 million without having some explanation as to how it is going to be spent.

It is largely due to the
accelerated naval program for the building of additional ships. It covers the procurement of major equipment, the building of additional ships, armament, signal and wireless, aircraft, mechanical equipment including transport, special training equipment, machinery, anti-submarine and electrical equipment. The estimate for ships and aircraft for this year is $74,610,000; for machinery, $800,000; for mechanical equipment including transport, $1,497,000; for armament equipment, $11,163,480; for signal and wireless including anti-submarine and electrical equipment, $22,154,303; for special training equipment, $729,600.

Would the minister be able
to indicate which if any of those vessels now under construction will be commissioned this year?

No, I would not be in a
position to do that. It is expected that several will be launched, but how many will be commissioned will depend on the progress we are able to make.

Would the minister say how
many ships were commissioned during the last fiscal year?

Of the new construction
program, none.

Did we get any new ships at
all last year?
Yes. Ships out of reserve.
What were they; frigates?

The destroyers Crescent,
Crusader and Nootka came out of reserve and were commissioned.
Could the minister say whether any of the new anti-submarine vessels are going to be ready this year?
None will be ready, but some vtill be launched this year.
You mean the keels will be laid.

No; the keels of several have been laid, and several will be launched in the autumn of 1951, but none will be ready this year. These vessels are well in advance of any ships of their kind being designed or made anywhere we know of. They are the last word in this type of construction and we anticipate considerable modification and development in them in the course of construction.
I wonder if the minister could tell us when the first one was-

No, I could not; possibly
next summer.

What I am asking is when
the contract for the first anti-submarine vessel was given to a Canadian shipyard. It seems that ever since I have been here, when the minister was giving us the program for the navy he has always told us that right now Canada was going to get the last thing in anti-submarine vessels, and so on. I have been here over two years and we are still waiting for one of these vessels to be commissioned.

This is really a matter for
the Minister of Defence Production, but in the case of a new vessel of a particular type like this I should think that the minimum period for the production of the first ship would be three years. It has most complicated electronic and wireless equipment, as well as a type of machinery not yet manufactured in Canada. So we would anticipate at least three years for the production of the first vessel, and after that they would be produced faster. I think we are at least a year ahead of any other country I know of in this field.

A considerable amount of money has been spent on advertising to secure men for the forces. It has been drawn to my attention that a young man who entered the army at the age of 15 or 16, who served a good many years-I believe he had only three years to serve before he was pensionable-was discharged with exemplary service. At the age of 35 he has again applied for enlistment, and has been refused. He went overseas into Brest and back again.
I am just wondering why that should be when we need men. He is a man with 15 or 16 years' experience in the army. He found out later that men who had been court-mar-tialled for different things overseas were returned to Canada and retained in the army, while he was discharged and has since been refused admission to the army. Would the minister say something about that?

If the hon. member would
give me the name of the individual concerned, I should be delighted to look into the matter and give him a full explanation. In the absence of the facts, I could not possibly deal with it on a hypothetical basis.

I shall give
the minister the name. It is Mr. E. W. S. Forrest.

I should like to know from
the minister if the people earning civil salaries and wages in the army are under the chief of staff.

The civilians in the three
services are attached to a local office or station establishment of the navy, army or air force, and come under the instructions of the immediate commander of the station or office to which they are attached. The commander, in turn, is responsible to the chief of staff, so remotely they come under the chief of staff. From the point of view of arrangements for employment, conditions of work, relations with the civil service commission, promotion and so on, they come under the deputy minister.

I thank the hon. minister
for his explanation. I have something to say about the chief of staff, who has rendered valuable service and who can be pensioned. I mean General Foulkes. It would be easy to replace him by one of the most distinguished officers of the British army or in the whole world; I mean General Alexander who is now our governor general. I do not say that merely because he is a man for whom I have great admiration, but because of his competence. As General Eisenhower is in charge of the United Nations troops in Europe, it would be a fine gesture to have General Alexander appointed as the

Supply-National Defence chief of staff. It would not make much difference because at the present time, as governor general, he is commander in chief of the Canadian army. It could be easily done. We would have someone of exceptional ability, a man who is diplomatic. There are very few people who will nat recognize that both General Eisenhower and General Alexander have the same ability.
This is my suggestion to the minister, who is the best minister since Mr. E. M. Macdonald, who was in charge of the department when I came here. We have now the best Minister of National Defence that I have known since I have been a member. I should like to have as chief of staff the best general that I know.

I do appreciate the words of the hon. member. I join with him in his appreciation of His Excellency, whose name I understand we are not supposed to mention in this house, but on this occasion I certainly join in the member's appreciation of him as an officer. I do not know how he would entertain the suggestion.

Civilian allowances. $10,000.

I suppose this is as good an
item as any under which to make the few remarks I have to make at this moment. They more or less concern some of the remarks that were made this afternoon by the member for Three Rivers. I heard the member, and I should like the minister to understand that on this side of the house there is at least one member if not more, but I can speak only for myself, who shares the views expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Three Rivers concerning the advisability of a French language college for the services, and his remarks as to the proportion of officers of French origin in the Canadian army. The minister answered that in peacetime it was not apparent that a career in the armed forces was very attractive to French-speaking Canadians. He may have said more of the truth than he thought when he said that, because many would have liked to join, many had splendid records during the war, but when peacetime came they could not get a commission in the regular forces. Many of those who did felt that they were not very happy.
I do not want to make this into a question of nationality or language only, but I think in all fairness to the people of Canada a better effort should be made towards greater participation by officers of French origin in the armed forces. The minister stated that some French-Canadian officers got a promotion at an early age. It may be that some of them

did, but so very few could get in that it does not change the picture much when we come to consider the proportion. The minister stated that they could get in, had they wanted to do so. I should like to know where they could have served. If I understand the matter correctly, it was only in Quebec at the citadel where the 22nd regiment was situated, where French-Canadian officers were taken in, and in Montreal in one of the regiments. That is as far as the active army was concerned before we had the Korean episode or the war in Korea. Frankly, I believe that the minister intends to do something, and I think the minister in the past has intended to do something. I will go so far as to say that I believe his present deputy minister is sympathetic toward the situation, but we need more than sympathy. I think that more positive gestures should be made.
I personally know of a group of young men who served gallantly during the first war and who were turned down when they tried to make a career in the army. Some of them had earned promotions in the field, had obtained higher rank, but when it came to ' getting in the army in peacetime they were told they did not have this or that university diploma and they were not considered acceptable for peacetime duties. Yet when some of these men got back to civilian life, they made a career and became prominent citizens in the field they had chosen. Surely the army could have accepted some of those people.
When you see here in Ottawa the list of officers serving at headquarters, the list of junior officers, the list of messengers, and the list of those in any category in the Department of National Defence, I do not think it is quite correct to come and say that the proportion is fair. I say this to the minister because we may be at a time when we shall again have to consider as most valuable the unity of all Canadians. The fact that Canadians of French descent enlisted so well in the reserves at the present request of the minister proves that they a're willing to do their share. But their share should not be done only when they are under fire. When, in peacetime, the army is reorganized I feel that they should be given a fair chance of promotion. Maybe I am wrong, but by looking at the list of headquarters staff very closely I could not find many French names. Maybe those included in the proportion mentioned by the minister are hidden somewhere.
Is this in order, Mr. Chairman?

Nevertheless, I say that there should be improvement in this regard.

The hon. member for Three Rivers advocated a college for the services which would be open to officers speaking the French language and where the lectures or tuition would be given in French. Whether it is given entirely in French or whether it is bilingual, as the minister has suggested, I think that a college catering especially to young men from French Canada who have the necessary education might serve us well if the time comes-and it may come sooner than we think-when we again have need for greater unity. If you have such a college, and if you have trained these young men, you might find a great many more who would join and who would feel that they can get a career in the army not only under fire but also in peacetime.
I do not want to extend these remarks at this moment, late in the session, but I want the minister to feel that on this side of the house there are also some people who share the views expressed by the hon. member for Three Rivers.

Very briefly I should like to associate my views with those of the previous speaker and of the hon. member for Three Rivers. I think it would be well worth while to give consideration to the possibility of establishing such a service college.
But there is a point I wanted to raise under this item. It covers pay and allowances of the active army which would be those forces of the army which are now in Korea; the forces which are now being assembled and trained for the 27th brigade; and the forces that are to remain in the country, in the active army, for the protection of Canada, those generally termed the airborne brigade and other units associated with them. It would also include those reinforcements that we have available both in Korea and for any other operation that might be undertaken.
I do not want the minister to stretch the dictates of security in any way at all, but I feel that the country would be interested in having a statement now giving some indication as to how the recruiting campaign has gone for the 27th brigade, and to what extent it has been necessary to transfer personnel from the airborne unit or the units of the airborne brigade and other permanent force units into the 27th brigade. I should also like to have a clear statement as to the number of reinforcements or replacements that there are available to meet any situation that might occur in Korea. Perhaps the minister could give us a statement with regard to that matter.

I am extremely glad to accept the opportunity extended by the question of the hon. member for Nanaimo. With regard to Korea, I had thought that the unusual circumstances that a Canadian unit had received a presidential citation for extreme heroism, as was announced in Korea the day before yesterday, might enable me to obtain the unanimous consent of the committee to put the citation on the records of the House of Commons, without reading it at length. This is the first time in the history of our country that this has happened, as far as I know; and the citation is in such language that I think every Canadian can be truly proud of the magnificent heroism shown by one of our greatest and proudest regiments.
I refer to the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Has the minister the unanimous consent of the committee to put this citation on Hansard?
Agreed.
Why should the minister not read it to us? It seems to me that would be the proper thing to do.

I can read it if there is no objection to my putting it on Hansard. The presidential citation reads as follows:
"3d battalion, Royal Australian Regiment.
2d battalion. Princess Pats Canadian Light Infantry and Company A, 72d heavy tank battalion (United States) are cited for extraordinary heroism and outstanding performance of combat duties in action against the armed enemy near Kapyong, Korea, on the 24th and 25th of April, 1951. The enemy had broken through the main line of resistance and penetrated to the area north of Kapyong. The units listed above were deployed to stem the assault. Early on the 24th of April, the 3d battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, moved to the right flank of the sector and took up defensive positions north of the Pukhon river.
The 2d battalion, Princess Pats Canadian Light Infantry, defended in the vicinity of Hill 677 on the left flank, Company A, 72d heavy tank battalion, supported all units to the full extent of its capacity and in addition, kept the main roads open and assisted in evacuating the wounded.
Troops from a retreating division passed through the sector which enabled enemy troops to infiltrate with the withdrawing forces. The enemy attacked savagely under the glamour of bugles and trumpets.
The forward elements were completely surrounded going through the first day and into the second. Again and again the enemy threw waves of troops at the gallant defenders and many times succeeded in penetrating the outer defences, but each time the courageous, indomitable and determined soldiers repulsed the fanatical attacks.
Ammunition ran low and there was no time for food. Critical supplies were dropped by air to the encircled troops, but still they stood their ground in resolute defiance of the enemy.
With serene and indefatigable persistence, the gallant soldiers held their defensive positions and took heavy tolls of the enemy. In some instances when the enemy penetrated the defences, the commanders directed friendly artillery fire on their own positions in repelling the thrusts.

Supply-National Defence
Toward the close of the second day, the 25th of April, the enemy breakthrough had been stopped. The seriousness of the breakthrough on the central front had been changed from defeat to victory by the gallant stand of these heroic and courageous soldiers.
The 3rd battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, 2nd battalion, Princess Pats Canadian Light Infantry, and Company A, 72nd Heavy Tank Battalion, displayed such gallantry, determination and esprit de corps in accomplishing their missions under extremely difficult and hazardous conditions as to set them apart and above other units participating in the campaign, and by their achievements they have brought distinguished credit on themselves, their homelands, and all freedom-loving nations.
Good old Canadians!
Has the minister received the official citation, or is this a newspaper report?
This is the official citation made by the general officer commanding in the field, which was communicated to the president and confirmed by him and which will be received by us in due course.

And permission will be
granted to the regiment to carry that citation?

Certainly. The hon. member for Nanaimo asked for some figures on the recruiting and strength of the Canadian army at the present time. As at June 25, 1951- again this is an estimate only in respect to the days in June-the army had 3,860 officers and 39,260 men, a total strength of 43,120.
Recruiting for the army showed the following results for this calendar year to June 25: January, 1,545; February, 1,132; March, 999; April, 709; May 6,171; June, 2,530; bringing the total number of recruits for the period, which is approximately the first six months of the calendar year, to 13,086.
With regard to the strength of the 25th Canadian infantry brigade group in Korea, subject to fluctuations in battle, which the hon. member appreciates, it has been up to strength. There are reinforcements to replace all casualties that we may suffer that could not be met by troops dispatched in the interval. In addition at estimated rates of casualties, we believe we have enough reinforcements trained or in training which, with those in Korea, would enable us to look after requirements for five or six months without further additions, although additions are being made from day to day.
Reinforcements in Korea?

In Korea or at Wainwright.
With regard to the 27th Canadian infantry brigade group, the results of the campaign have been largely due to the fine co-operation of the 42 units of the reserve army. Up to

four o'clock yesterday afternoon, 8,384 officers and men have been taken on strength, and that is considerably more than the original intended strength of the intended force to be sent to Europe. Recruiting is continuing.
That would not include men who have been taken on and discharged? We can take it as being the approximate strength of the brigade?

That is the total number of recruits. The number of men released is 567. In addition there are about 1,600 men who have applied and who have not yet been examined. So that one can say that out of the applications so far made the strength of this brigade group will be approximately 9,000 or more, which will provide very substantial replacements of officers and men for rotation.
With regard to the strength of the forces in Canada, it has not been the practice to give break-downs of the forces especially earmarked for the defence of our country and others in detail, but I can tell the hon. member that at the present time the field force, the active force brigade group, as it is called, is very well on the way to full strength. It has replaced largely the men who left it to join the 25th Canadian infantry brigade group. Its strength at the present time is in excess of 5,000. For the first time in the history of Canada, we have in operational forces, in fighting formations, in the active force brigade group, the 25th Canadian infantry brigade group in Korea, and the 27th Canadian infantry brigade group, in coast and antiaircraft batteries, in artillery units, in the reinforcement and replacement forces, and in other formations of more static troops such as engineers, army service corps and so on, about all the organization necessary for a division. As a matter of fact, we have in the magnitude of 28,000 to 30,000 operational troops at the present time. In other words about two-thirds of the Canadian army at the present time can be said to be operational.

Before we get too far away from the citation which the minister read, I think it is fitting that it should be put into Hansard that the members of the House of Commons on the whole were enthusiastic in their applause when this citation was read.

The statements that have been made are general statements in regard to the strength of the forces. The statements seem to reflect the idea that we are dealing with this in terms of peace; otherwise the statements would have no meaning,

in view of the fact that we have had such large forces on other occasions when we faced more serious conditions.
The Guardian of the Gulf, a newspaper published in Charlottetown, in its issue of Saturday, June 23, carried a report of a speech by the Postmaster General, and I find these words in that speech:
We have so worked with other Atlantic pact countries as to be sure Russia would be defeated if she attacked today.
In view of certain statements made by senior staff officers in the United States, which do not indicate quite the same opinion, I would ask the Minister of National Defence whether he shares the view expressed by the Postmaster General in these words last Friday.

I certainly believe that
Russia would be defeated if she attacked today or at any other future date. I believe that the resources of the western democracies, and of those that would be associated with them in an all-out war, would defeat the forces of the Soviet union and those that they could muster. However, my object is not to defeat Russia, although I certainly would do everything possible to do it- and would succeed, I believe, with others, should that come about.
Our object is to prevent war by deterring aggression, by building up our forces to the point where an aggressor will hesitate to attack. That is why we are in Korea, and that is why we are in the North Atlantic treaty. That is why the other western nations are devoting such huge proportions of their national effort and national income to the job we have set our hands to.
If the leader of the opposition-

speechtext: Order. I must point out that we are discussing a subitem for pay and allowances, to the amount of $86,583,800. A question has been asked regarding a matter that was dealt with when we had the discussion on the general item.

I do not see why an answer would not be in order. After all we want to know what results we are getting for the money we are laying out. Before going further may I congratulate the Minister of National Defence upon his confidence. I trust

With the help of the Lord!

As the Postmaster General has raised the question, I would point out that either we have a tremendous task ahead of us, or we have not. We know that there is only one possible enemy. We know that possible enemy has been preparing, and preparing carefully for many years.

speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the leader of the opposition; but, notwithstanding opinions which have been expressed by the hon. member for Lethbridge, and in the opening remarks of the leader of the opposition, when he was returning to the subject because the Postmaster General had risen on a question of privilege, I cannot see how we can discuss policy on a subitem relating to pay and allowances.

That creates complete disorder. I would ask hon. members to carry on in the manner agreed upon, and confine their remarks to the subitem under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to debate your ruling. I would point out that we are dealing with an item of more than $86 million out of a total of more than $116 million involving the army. This $86 million is for pay and allowances for the army. I want to know what we are getting for that amount of money, and it is in relation to that I am asking the question. However, if you rule this is not the appropriate point, there are two or three other obvious points where I could ask the question later. If you feel that it should be deferred, I will accept your ruling. But I will certainly come back to it.

Subitem agreed to.
Pensions, superannuation and other benefits in respect of personal services, $203,400.

I should like to say a few words on this item. The minister and others who served on the defence committee will recall that I raised this question in committee, and I also raised it in the house on one other

Supply-National Defence occasion. I shall make my remarks as brief as possible because I want to know if the minister or the department has done anything about this problem I brought to their attention.
This has to do with members of the permanent force who pay in to the superannuation fund. The case I brought specifically to their attention was that of a captain who had served about ten years in the permanent force, who had paid into the superannuation fund, who suffered a heart attack and died while in the service. He left a widow and two children. The widow could never establish pension rights because the ruling was that his death was not attributable to service, as such. War veterans allowance could not be established for her because she was not sixty years of age and was not considered incapacitated.
The particular feature about it, and the one having special reference to this matter of superannuation, is that the money paid in by the soldier, in the expectation that it would protect his family in the event of his death, was refunded to her in a lump sum. The income tax department deducted $650 from that money, for income tax purposes.
I brought this to the attention of the Minister of Finance. I have written to the Department of National Revenue. I took it up with the committee that considered defence matters recently, and! I was of the opinion that the deputy minister, when the matter was brought to his attention in the committee, was somewhat shocked to think that that would take place in connection with superannuation arrangements of service personnel.
This matter has been under consideration for at least eighteen months by the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of National Defence. I am wondering if the department has done any thinking' about the matter, and if any arrangements have been made with the Department of Finance to ascertain whether the widow, whose husband gave gallant service and1 who died; in the service of the permanent force, leaving his family totally unprotected, should be deprived of this $650. This is taken from the superannuation moneys paid in by the soldier while he was in the service.
This seems to be a loose arrangement, and one in connection with which some concrete legislation should be enacted. There is very little encouragement for a man in the service when he realizes that that sort of thing can happen to his family. I know the pension commission has rejected the pension claim for disability purposes. The Department of Veterans Affairs has turned down the widow
[Mr. Gillis.l
because she is not old enough, and she is not incapacitated. But she has two children to look after and a home to maintain, which I think incapacitates the average woman from getting out and earning a living. That angle is not taken into consideration, but I suggest to the Minister of National Defence that he should get in touch with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue, and that some arrangement should be made with those departments to relieve that type of income for tax purposes. I believe that widow should be reimbursed the money collected from her by the Department of National Revenue.

I should like to associate myself with the hon. member who has just taken his seat. If the boys whose gallantry we heard of tonight had placed the dollar sign first, rather than human values first, as spectacularly as the Department of National Revenue has placed the dollar sign before human values, we should have heard no such citation as we heard tonight.
Can the minister not answer the question put to him by the hon. member for Cape Breton South? It is a very shocking set of circumstances.

I would be very glad to give an answer if it were possible for me to do so. It is a case I have heard of only tonight, but I will be glad to draw it to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue. It does not seem to be a matter for this department except from a general interest point of view to see that the rights and interests of those who serve, and their dependents, are looked after.

Would the minister not only draw it to their attention but tell them what ought to be done? Certainly this kind of thing is most reprehensible. I doubt very much if ten per cent of the people of Canada would favour that sort of thing. Surely we should have a little more than drawing attention.

I am rather surprised to hear the minister say that this matter has not been brought to his attention. If he will look at the records of the committee that studied the defence bill he will find I made a complete statement on the matter, a little longer than the one I made tonight. His deputy minister was there, and one of his parliamentary assistants was chairman of the committee. I think someone in his department should have taken a look at the record and should have drawn the matter to his attention. I really expected the Department of National Defence to go after the Department of

National Revenue to see if some arrangement could not be made for the refund of that money to the widow in the circumstances I have described.

1 feel like the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I think the minister should not be "drawing" matters like this to the attention of these men. He should be "telling" them what to do. If he is going to be charged with the responsibility of conducting the affairs of national defence of this nation he must not have colleagues of his under his feet or clinging to his skirts and making his position impossible. If matters of that sort get abroad among the forces to any great extent, I would not be surprised if a good deal of enthusiasm for the cause would be thereby destroyed.

Subitem agreed to.
Reserve force (including Canadian officers' training corps)-
Pay and allowances, $8,000,000.
First of all I should like the minister to tell us how many reserve army personnel this vote is intended to cover, and what the strength of the reserve army is at the present time.
The strength of the reserve force at the 30th of April was 46,626. This item would provide for the payment of an average throughout the year of 48,000.
How does that figure compare with twelve months ago?
Twelve months ago there were 43,584.
Can the minister tell us how many were at reserve force camps last year and how many are expected to go to camp this year?
Last year there were 12,000. Provision is made this year for 16,000.

I, somewhat fail to understand these figures. The minister stated earlier this year, and as a matter of fact has been stating for some time, that every effort was going to be made to increase the strength of the reserve force, and especially the effective strength. However, apparently the estimates were prepared with the expectation that the strength of the reserve force would not be very much more than it is at the present time or more than what it has been for the last year or two. I should like to ask the minister what steps, if any, are being taken to increase the strength of the reserve force, particularly their effective strength. The figure of 46,626, which the minister mentioned, is of course the number of men on the rolls of the reserve force units, 80709-304
Supply-National Defence and I think the minister will admit that the rolls bear very little relation to the effective strength of the units because a large number of these men turn out very infrequently for drill, and they do not get to summer camp.
While they are on the rolls, they can hardly be counted as the effective strength of a unit. I think it has been admitted by practically everyone having anything to do with the reserve, or the army generally, that one of the things we need in this country is a larger, stronger and more effective reserve force. Up to the present time I have not noted any signs that the government is taking any really effective steps to produce larger and better reserve forces.

During the last three years, speaking from memory but referring to the white paper, the size of the reserve force has increased by approximately 40 per cent. I will verify that in a moment. During the fiscal year 1950-51 a total of no less than 268 officers and 3,198 men of the reserve forces or a grand total of 3,406 joined the Canadian army active force, including the 25th brigade now Korea. From April 1 to May 31 of this year 170 officers and 1,730 men of the reserves or a total of 1,900 more joined the active army. The total number of officers and men who, during this seventeen-month period, have joined the active army from the reserves is 5,366. That is a substantial contribution indeed by the reserve forces of Canada to the active force at this time, and I am sure everyone is very glad that the reserve forces have responded so well. It is no part of the job of the reserve forces of Canada to be ready to meet a fully trained and equipped enemy in battle tomorrow. That is not their role. Their job is to provide support for the active forces, which they are doing magnificently, and a nucleus of trained officers and N.C.O.'s and as many tradesmen and men as possible on which to build rapidly in the event of an emergency.
Everything possible that has been suggested by the reserve force associations except exemption from income tax I think has been carried out, and if hon. members have any further ideas on ways and means of assisting in this work I would be glad to hear them. As far as we can ascertain we are doing everything possible to support the reserve forces and enable them to carry out their job better than ever before. From the point of view of armoury accommodation, for example, it has been increased by 100 per cent since 1939. I think the hon. member for Calgary East will know from his own experience how the conditions of service, training and equipment have been improved. If hon. members know of anything more that can be done we

Supply-National Defence would be glad to consider it. We are in very-close communication with the reserve army units and the units of the other reserve forces, and every suggestion they make is actively pursued.

The minister says everything possible is being done, and he would like any further suggestions. I would suggest for one thing that those units that have had equipment taken away, either to be sent to Europe or for use by the regular forces, should be given either the same type of equipment or whatever new equipment they are to have. I should like to know whether units that have lost equipment for these purposes have had that equipment made good yet.

I am informed that no unit lacks equipment with which to do the training it is capable of doing. The only equipment removed that I know of was some self-propelled guns on tracks which were replaced temporarily by 25-pounders or other weapons in order to enable us to complete the shipments to Europe in full divisions. We are beginning to receive from the United States equipment to replace what was shipped abroad. It will not be issued to reserve army units first, but they have plenty of equipment with which to train.

Then the minister drew a red herring across the trail by saying it is no part of the role of the reserve forces to be able to mobilize immediately to meet any emergency, that they are not supposed to be trained to the point where they could turn out and fight tomorrow. No one said they were; that was never mentioned. The minister indicated some of the other roles of the reserve forces, however, and the difficulty is that they are not able to meet those other roles. That has been my criticism. A large number of units of the reserve forces just have not sufficient men to be able to carry on training. As a result their good officers and N.C.O.'s are to a large extent wasting their time because they have no men to train with. Many of them are becoming discouraged as a result and attend parades infrequently or quit.

The figures away back in that period are considerably larger than the number of men in the reserve forces at the present time, in spite of the fact that the population of Canada today is several million more than it was then, and in spite of the fact that world conditions are certainly much graver now than they were then. My own experience, and that of most other men I have spoken to who have served in the reserve forces, is that the reserve force is not nearly as good now as it was back in this period. I think the number of men in the reserve forces should be much greater, while actually it is smaller. It is no good for the minister to make the general statement that we are doing everything possible to create a strong reserve force. If they have not adopted the right method they have failed. The report of the council of the defence forces, made up of men in the reserve units-it is no use putting it on the record again, since it has been read here a couple of times already-stated in very blunt terms that they were not able to do a job because they just did not have the men to do it efficiently.

Has the department any agreement or understanding with employers across the country as to whether leave of absence is granted men for the purpose of attending summer camp? I brought this matter to the attention of the minister a few months ago, when I pointed out that at least one large employer of labour last year did not grant leave of absence to men who went to summer camp with the reserve army. Those men were classified as absentees, which injured them in many ways. In addition they lost a bonus which accumulates as the result of study work. I have written to the department again as far as that company is concerned, and I know the deputy minister is working on it. But I know many years ago when I went to camp all I had to do was go to my employer and inform him I was taking two or three weeks off to go to camp to the reserve army. It does not appear as if that is the situation today. Is there any official understanding on that point?

In each of the last four
years we have taken up with both representatives of employers, the Canadian chamber

of commerce, and employees, the trade unions and others, the desirability of getting full co-operation in facilitating the men going to camp. Each year I write to every major employer in Canada. This year some 3,500 letters went forward, and I received a very good response. So far this year I have only heard of one Arm failing to co-operate and that case has been handed over to the minister in that particular province. He is going to take it up with the firm concerned. The year before last I heard of another firm, and found that it happened to have a government contract. I made some representations to my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and that situation was speedily rectified. Those are the only two cases of which I know. The hon. member has drawn another case to our attention, and we are looking into that. So far we have had good co-operation from employers right across Canada. A great number of them not only grant leave of absence, but make up the differential in pay during that period.
Answering the hon. member for Calgary East, it should be recognized that the figure he gave for 1925-26 was for reserve forces When the strength of the active force was 4,334. The total strength of the active and reserve forces that year was 54,395. At this time it is in excess of 133,000, so that a lot of young men who used to be in the reserve forces are now in the active forces. I do not agree for one second that either one or the other was as effective as today.

I want to speak very briefly
on this matter of reserve units. It has been discussed before so far as my province is concerned. The minister has expressed himself as toeing quite satisfied with the units as recruited at the present time. I do want to ask him once again-I do this not on my own but at the request of the commanding officers of the reserve units- to have an active service unit with a Newfoundland name established in Newfoundland. The minister is fully cognizant of the value of Newfoundland recruits. I am sorry, but every province in Canada has not got an active service unit associated with it They are dominion wide. There is the Royal Canadian Regiment, the Royal 22ieme and the P.P.C.L.I., in the infantry, and the R.C.D.'s and Lord Stratheona's. The question of stationing an active force unit in Newfoundland is under consideration for some future date.

Order. I am
sorry to interrupt the leader of the opposition, but on a similar subitem, which was discussed previously and carried, he attempted to make a similar statement. I indicated then that, in my view, a discussion of collective security and matters of policy was not relevant to the subitem under discussion. The same ruling I made a moment ago applies now. I shall expect all hon. members to relate their remarks to the subitem under discussion which is pay and allowances, subitem 3, $8 million.

Mr. Chairman, we are dealing with a subitem that has to do with the training of men who are apparently to be trained for some purpose; and there is not a single hon. member in this committee who does not know what that purpose is. I shall not repeat the name of the nation which has indicated the reason to all of us why this training has, or should have, some measure of reality. As to the statements that have been made and the answers that have been given, I suggest that, having regard to the nature of the threat that everyone knows exists today, we are dealing with this subject in an atmosphere of complete pretence and unreality. Either this reserve force is being built up with the idea that it will be an effective reserve for the kind of operation that this country might be called upon to accept as part of its obligation or else we are simply going on during a period of comparative peace in which the figures of expenditure before us would be wholly unjustified.

I prefer to believe that the figures before us interpret the nature of the threat and the scale of the responsibility that this country has assumed. I suggest that as we discuss the training of the reserve forces which have been described as the basis of our whole defence organization, we must do so with an acceptance of the fact that, short of war itself, this country never faced a greater threat than it faces at this hour.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think that I have given as much consideration as I possibly could to the possible relevancy of the remarks that are being made by the leader of the opposition on this subitem. I am sorry to interrupt him again, but I do not think that on this subitem he should embark upon a general discussion of the purpose for which the Canadian reverve army is being trained and organized.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, you might indicate under what subitem in connection with the reserve forces it would be appropriate to discuss the role they are expected to occupy.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The chairman, of course, is not here to indicate to hon. members what they should discuss and how they should discuss whatever they want to put forward. The chairman is here to decide questions of order whenever they arise.

The training of the reserve is being carried on, as has already been pointed out, at a level much lower in percentage of the actual force available than took place in the years when we accepted the belief that we were at peace. I can best illustrate my point by taking a particular unit which is illustrative of many others. Let me take as an illustration an artillery regiment. An artillery regiment would have a normal strength of approximately 600 men. At the present time an artillery regiment well up to strength, by comparison, has probably 120 to 140 men. When that regiment goes to Petawawa camp for training it will take 40 men. Because of the fact that it has been one of the units supplying men for the special force under the recruiting arrangements that recently have been made, it will not find it possible to take trained N.C.O. personnel up to its establishment. We therefore find that, in a period when the training at least is important, the unit will be taking 40 instead of 60 men to that kind of training which gives it some measure of understanding of active force training.
There is alternative training all throughout Canada for artillery units, infantry units and other units. There is local training in the headquarters and there is also training in

camps in the districts themselves. In the particular district which I have in mind by way of illustration, there is an artillery training camp at Meaford. There it is possible for artillery units within that area to carry out active firing practice; and that is the place where units of that kind get the kind of training that prepares them for service conditions. I am taking that only as an example, and I have reason to believe that a similar situation is found elsewhere across Canada, not only with respect to the artillery but with respect to other services.
The particular unit to which I referred applied for the opportunity to train at the Meaford artillery camp at week ends, where they could take the unit to camp and obtain the kind of firing practice that gives a measure of reality to artillery training. They have been informed in this year, which we are told is the most critical year of the period of training, that they may expect to have a week end of training next October. That is the atmosphere in which training is being carried out, and the sense of reality in connection with it.
As we deal with these figures, and if we accept the statement of the Minister of National Defence that the reserve is the basis of our whole army strength, with these figures before us, I submit that this matter is not being approached in the terms of reality which should be present. I do not think anything could illustrate that statement better than the break-down of the items appearing in the public accounts during the year 1949-50. Those are, unfortunately, the last that are available to us. They indicate the manner in which training has been carried out even at a time when it was considered that there were threats that it was necessary for us to face. In those details, which are available to all the members of this committee, it was disclosed that the amount expended during that period for ammunition and bombs was $2,166,493.11 whereas the amount spent for printing and stationery was $2,345,854.01. In other words, $200,000 more was spent for printing and stationery than was spent for ammunition and bombs which would make it possible to carry out the training of the reserve force and the other forces in this country.
Mr. Chairman, if this country in fact faces the necessity of training men to face whatever they might be called upon to face within the armed forces of Canada, I suggest that we should no longer have the generalities that we receive, that we should no longer be going on in the casual, easy way that we are proceeding, training men at summer camps and throughout the year as though this was
Supply-National Defence a settled period of peace; training only 25 per cent of the low number that are being trained at all in reserve units; and training only approximately 12 per cent of the number actually permitted by the treasury board, according to the evidence given a few weeks ago. Rather, I submit that we should say that this threat is one which calls not only for the expenditure of $1,500 million but also for the training of men with an acceptance of the reality in front of us.
I believe that every member in this house is ready to support expenditures that are to be made for the kind of results that all of us would desire, and would train the men for the one purpose that brings them into uniform. We all want peace, we all respect and admire the young men in uniform; but I believe that it is the job of this parliament to see that with the huge expenditures that we are making we are going to provide these young men with the kind of training that will make it possible for them to meet whatever test they may be called upon to face.

Subitem agreed to.
Acquisition and construction of buildings and works, including acquisition of land, $3,247,000.

On May 10 when we were in committee the minister said that the accommodation for the reserve army had been increased by over 100 per cent in the last five years. On March 16, 1950, I had a question on the order paper which reads as follows:
What armouries, drill halls and urban training centres for the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian army, or the Royal Canadian Air Force are at present under construction in Canada?
The answer I got from the parliamentary assistant to the minister was: "The Canadian army, an armoury at Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario." I wonder whether the minister can relate these two statements because they are rather confusing to me. Can he point out where the 99 per cent increase, which I suppose is being shown here in this item, is being spent?

The difference, as the hon. member must anticipate, is in the purchase of existing buildings and the conversion of wartime construction where that has been possible. For example, at Winnipeg there are some eight or ten reserve units stationed in wartime constructed buildings. In Montreal, for example, the seven units of the Royal Canadian army medical corps and the Royal Canadian dental corps are now housed in a building we exchanged for another building. This is situated on St. Urban street; RCEME and engineers are now located in a large building situated on St. James street in the west of the city; and so on. We have bought a large number of buildings across Canada.

Supply-National Defence We thought it was the desirable thing to do. It is much cheaper than building, and it provided units with accommodation they badly needed.
How about the division of this $3 million odd?
Purchase of real property, land and buildings, $185,000; construction, major contract projects, $2,556,000; construction, day labour, minor contract projects, $506,000.
We would like to know the locations, please.

I am afraid I cannot give that until they are approved by council, which is not yet given. The largest single item of expenditure will be at Sault Ste. Marie, to complete the large single armoury there.
With regard to matters that have not yet been approved, I am not in a position to give their locations.
The minister cannot say where this money is to be spent for large units?
It has not been approved by the cabinet and treasury board yet. The location of each of these places is not selected.

I must say that I thought the minister was coming here and asking us to approve expenditures for definite things. Now we cannot tell what this money is going to be spent for, because it has not been approved by some other body.
For reserve army accommodation.
Very, very generous.

Mr. Chairman, in Lethbridge we believe that we ought to have a large armoury. We have a number of reasons which make us believe that the armoury in Lethbridge ought to have priority. We do not wish to be selfish, but we are a rapidly growing community and we are in a strategic position. Will the minister tell us just about what the situation is with respect to building an armoury at Lethbridge?

The hon. member for Nanaimo will appreciate more my position as he hears the question of the hon. member for Lethbridge. A very large number of hon. members have suggested that it would be desirable to have armouries built in their localities, and until it is actually decided to build it and the contract is about to be let we simply cannot announce it. Lethbridge, like a good many other places, is on the list of localities where an armoury is considered to be desirable and needed. It is a question of priority. In the province of Alberta there are about ten places

where we would like to build armouries just as soon as we have the money, the materials and the labour to go ahead. Lethbridge is one of them. Beyond that I cannot give any assurance to the hon. member. It is very high on the list.

Would it assist the minister if we all put forward the advantages of the various places where we live and where we have units so that he could let whatever body he is going to refer it to reach a decision.
Thank you.

It is only fair that hon. members should know something about the reasons why Lethbridge is of importance in this matter. Lethbridge is located on the road that would connect the United States with the Alaska highway. Lethbridge is not very far away from the United States border. There is an excellent place there for training. Lethbridge is on what will be the southernmost route of the trans-Canada highway when that route is completed, and for these reasons I personally believe that it is in a highly strategic position, and I think the minister will agree with me. Consequently I feel that I am quite in order in presenting to hon. members and to the minister a request that Lethbridge should be strictly borne in mind.
Thank you; that will be considered.

If this is the way that these estimates are prepared then we might as well admit that this whole procedure is fantastic nonsense. It is certainly elementary that when the government comes before us and asks us to approve expenditures, it has already itself approved of the purpose for which the money is asked. In these cases where there cannot be specific approval then it may well be that some contingency fund may be set up, as is the case for instance in the Department of National Health and Welfare, to meet obligations of this kind which they actually cannot anticipate in advance. But to come to this House of Commons and to say that the government has not yet approved of any of the things for which these expenditures are asked is a complete denial of the whole fundamental principle upon which the preparation of estimates is based. And if we are called upon to pass this item with no more information than we now have, then we might as well accept the proposition that the passing of these items is a complete farce, from here on.
