Supply-National Defence informed that a decision has not yet been reached to produce rifles and machine guns in our own plants. Therefore I am curious to know how it is possible to expect that we will build anything like this, if we have not yet decided on the weapons to be used.
It is that kind of uncertainty which leads us to introduce the 15 per cent factor.

The 15 per cent factor would be a very small factor if in fact we are not going to have the weapons this year. If we have not started to make them yet we will not have new weapons this year. Cannot the minister give us an estimate of what he expects will be spent?

We are buying a large proportion of the weapons for the first two divisions from the United States. Delivery has already commenced on that. We are buying a very considerable proportion of the ammunition. How much of the ammunition and weapons, in addition to that for the two divisions, will be made in Canada, depends upon what orders can be obtained, and the economic rates of production. That is a matter for the Minister of Defence Production.

Subitem agreed to.
General; acquisition and construction of buildings and works, including acquisition of land, $75,526,500.
Does this item include the construction of an armoury and naval barracks, as we were promised last year? Surely out of one of these items we will get either of those buildings this year.

We have passed the items which would be applicable, but I know the hon. member is interested in the matter. It is not proposed in the near future to construct reserve army accommodation in Charlottetown, because the quality of the armoury at that point is well up. There are many places where the need is more urgent.
With regard to the navy, Charlottetown is one of the three places where we hope to construct new quarters for the naval reserve division. We are beginning this year in Regina. Charlottetown is one of the two remaining places. It is high on the list.
How is this $75 million being apportioned? Is the major portion for married quarters, for the construction of camps, or what is the purpose?

There is $910,000 for the purchase of lands; $68,441,500 for major contract projects; $3,825,000 for day labour and minor contract projects; and $2,350,000 for other acquisitions and construction. The major

Supply-National Defence amounts include $19,909,500 for married quarters; additional properties at Barriefield; Ottawa service accommodation; Calgary camp training area and Vancouver service area. This program provides for our spending a very considerable sum on prefabricated huts, which would be available to meet immediate needs and also for mobilization purposes.
You mean these prefabricated houses are not being placed anywhere at the moment? They are just in a prefabricated state ready to be put where needed?

Yes. The contract has not been placed yet. The appropriation has not been made. That accounts for $11 million. At Fredericton there is a small project. At Halifax there is an ordnance warehouse, $550,000; Bouchard, Longue Pointe, Montreal; Quebec, St. Malo; Quebec Citadel; Saint John, a barrack block and new mess hall; Barriefield, a barrack and mess hall, heating plant; Camp Borden, two barrack blocks and a mess hall; at Kingston a water and sewage system; London, a barrack block and garage; Meaford, general development; Ottawa, at the 26th O.D., two storage buildings; Petawawa, a large scale development, $1 million, a mess hall, and garage; Petawawa, heating plant; Picton, barrack block, water and sewage system; Churchill, further development, married quarters, laundry building; Dundurn, magazines; Rivers, a storage depot for air training equipment; Shilo, two barrack blocks and a garage; Winnipeg, an ordnance warehouse; Calgary, a barrack block and tank hangar; Chilliwack, stores and work shops covering storage for bridging equipment, central heating plant, water and sewage system; Edmonton, R.C.E. office, stores and work shops, supply depot, ordnance warehouse, central heating plant, water and sewage system; Victoria, a garage, radar building, recreation building; Vancouver, an ordnance warehouse, and at Wainwright a general scheme of development of over $2 million.

I take it that there is $19
million for married quarters, $11 million for prefabricated houses, and the rest of the vote, which would be $45 million, is for army camps, permanent barracks, and things of that kind.
That is right.

At the beginning the
minister mentioned something about Sarcee, but when he read the list Sarcee was not in it. I was wondering what there is in the vote for Sarcee.
It is the purchase of land at Sarcee now being used as the actual training area.
It is land you are going to buy from the Indians of the Sarcee Indian reserve?
Yes.
How much land is being purchased from them?
It is not the whole reserve.

The whole reserve is ten
miles wide by thirty miles long, so I would not think it would be that. Could the minister indicate how much of the reserve they are purchasing?

We want to purchase that
part of the Sarcee reserve which we are presently using as a range and practice ground. Speaking offhand, it is something under 500 acres.

Subitem agreed to.
Major procurement of equipment. $198,930,650.
This is a very large item. Would the minister indicate what are the major items of equipment that it covers?

Tanks and armoured fighting vehicles, $32,217,000; mechanical equipment including transport, $30,292,350; armament and equipment, $123,959,000; signal and wireless equipment, $12,262,000; and special training equipment, $200,300.

Over a month ago, when
we were discussing these estimates, in one of his speeches the minister said that equipment to replace that which we had sent overseas for one division would be secured within a month from the United States. Can the minister tell us if this equipment has in fact been secured by this time? It is more than a month since he made that statement.

Delivery has commenced.
It is starting to come in, and we expect it to roll in quite fast from now on. I think it has been coming for a couple of weeks.

If the minister does not think he should say so for security reasons it is all right, but if he can say so I should like to know whether there is equipment for more than one division coming in, or is it just proposed to secure equipment for one division?
Equipment for two divisions is on the way.

I should like to ask a question about a specific item of equipment, namely, artillery weapons. I have waited until we

reached the specific item instead of discussing it on the general item because it seems to me to be a particular problem. As a matter of interest, I should like to ask the minister whether any consideration has been given to the forces of ourselves, the United States and Great Britain using the German 88 millimetre gun which those of us who were on the receiving end of it in the last war found so extremely effective and unpleasant. Having discussed this matter with other servicemen, though not at all as experts, it seemed to us this was one place where we might well profit from what I believe was generally agreed to be the most useful all-round piece of artillery on either side during the war. Can the minister tell us whether any consideration has been given by any of the three countries I have mentioned to adopting it, or even preferably, to standardization on a gun of that type?

Yes, consideration has been given to that. The other countries concerned do not admit the generally acknowledged superiority of the 88, and for the time being the United States and ourselves will standardize on the 105. However, there is under development a weapon very superior to either the 88 or the 105.
Built by the United States?
I must not say.

I take it the minister prefers not to answer that. I do not wish to infringe on security. I wonder if I could put it this way. It seems to me that one of the most outstanding features of the 88 millimetre gun was its adaptability to a variety of purposes, as an anti-tank weapon, anti-personnel weapon and anti-aircraft weapon. The one gun had all three types of use. That would seem to me to be one reason particularly why we might use a weapon of that type. Is it considered that the type of weapon to which the minister has referred has this same feature of being useful for all three purposes?

I would not like to give the characteristics of the weapon and still less the one in process of development. I can say that the 3-inch 50-calibre naval gun, for example, that we are making at Sorel under an arrangement with the United States for the United States navy as well as our own navy has all these characteristics to which the hon. member has referred. I would think any weapon of the most modern type will have them.

Just so I may be clear, that 3-inch 50-calibre gun is for use by the navy, not the army?
Supply-National Defence
That is right.
From the minister's answer I take it that he does not care to go any further with respect to the new weapon which has been developed?
That is right.

I would like to know what is meant when the minister speaks of the 3-inch 50-calibre naval gun. If I asked the calibre of our present service rifle the minister would reply -303. From the description of this gun I should think the calibre would be 3 inch, but it is always described as 3-inch 50-calibre. What is the reason for that?

In our parlance we call this a 3-inch naval gun, but to identify it in contradistinction to other naval guns the Americans also indicate the length in the calibres, which is 50, which means the gun is 50 calibres or 150 inches long.

Subitem agreed to.
Repairs and upkeep of equipment, $24,042,650.

I do not know whether this is the proper item, but I would like to commend the minister and the department on the excellent manner in which they are keeping up the equipment at the Hagersville army camp. I would like to know if it is the intention to build any living accommodation for the personnel there.
No; that is not in the present project for married quarters.

Subitem agreed to.
Contributions, grants, subsidies, etc., not included elsewhere, $783,700.
I would like to know to whom these contributions or grants are made.

These are for grants to bands, libraries, Canadian officers training corps, reading rooms, messes, etc., made in accordance with regulations. I can give the details. In the active force, for example, there are twenty-four authorized bands receiving a grant of $500 each. In the reserve there are 79 bands of 15 pieces each receiving $150, 95 bands of 20 pieces at $200 each, 45 bands of 25 pieces at $250 each, and 130 bands of 30 pieces at $300 each. Library grants are for the active force, command and area libraries, staff college and school libraries; there is one at Halifax and one at R.M.C. Then for the C.O.T.C. there are grants to nine contingents of 48 members or less, $50 each, and so on. A grant of $20 is allowed for 100 reading rooms. Fifty officers' messes were allowed $360 a year. For schools of instruction there

Supply-National Defence is a grant of $100. There are contingency and training allowances for the reserved forces, $180,000; Canadian officers training corps, $2,500; contingent officers, $5,000. Training allowances for reserved forces and the C.O.T.C.; allowances for the care of arms; maintenance of physical fitness equipment, totalling $92,520. Here also are the allowances for the various reserve force units for clerical assistance and organization; grants and allowances for army cadets. Under the northwest highway system there are four different items of allowances. All these are provided in accordance with regulations on a uniform basis across the country.

Subitem agreed to.
Northwest highway system-
Civil salaries and wages, $845,800.

I notice an increase this year of something like $4,500,000. This highway is 1,221 miles in length. When you consider the airstrips and connecting roads, it may run to 1,500 miles. The expenditure this year is $12,637,700, which works out at about $8,400 a mile for the maintenance of a gravel road. After we took over this highway, in 1946-47 it cost us $3,642,769 to maintain it. In 1949-50 that cost had risen to $7,231,000. Last year it cost something over $8,200,000, and this year it has gone up to more than $12,600,000. This cost seems away out of line, unless a good deal of new construction is going to be carried on this year. We all want to see the Alaska highway maintained, but it seems to me it should not cost $8,400 a mile to maintain a gravel highway on which there is not very much traffic.
The hon. gentleman should know his facts before making statements which are liable to mislead the house.
I asked a question of the minister. I think I have as many facts in this report as the hon. member for Cariboo has, if not more.

The hon. member says there is not much traffic on the highway. For hundreds of miles that highway passes through the riding I have the honour to represent, and I want to say it is very heavily travelled by both civilian and military traffic. Further than that, the Alaska highway is the only link we have with the territory of Alaska. It is the life line upon which we would have to depend in the event of any attack upon the territory of Alaska. No doubt the money voted is being spent wisely, and the difficulty is that not enough is being voted. On the other side of the Yukon-Alaska boundary the United States is paving the

highway, making it a hard surfaced road. On our side we have a gravel highway, but it is being well maintained. It was left in good shape when the United States army pulled out, and under the Department of National Defence it has been well maintained'. I am sure too much attention could not be given to this life line of democracy in the northwestern part of 'this continent.

The hon. member has tried to completely misinterpret what I said. I was not saying anything against maintaining the Alaska highway. I was saying that the cost shown here of practically $10,000 a mile would go a long way toward paving it. It is this cost of upkeep that is out of line with similar costs anywhere else that I know of that I am asking about.

The fact is that the highway is being rebuilt here and there. Bridges are being added; it is being relocated and modernized. Of course the minister can answer the question, but representing that riding I think I have a right to refute any erroneous statements made with respect to the Alaska highway.

The largest single item in the increase between $8,133,268 for 1950-51 and the $12,637,700 for 1951-52 is on construction. This is largely for the continuation of a program of replacing wartime temporary construction, particularly wooden bridges and culverts that were put in by the United States forces during the war. In 1950 we started a program of replacing those with permanent bridges and culverts. Of this sum $3,281,000 is required to continue the work we began last year in the operation of making this into a permanent highway.
In addition, there are small items for the construction of a sewage system, a sewage disposal system and water storage and pumping facilities. At Nelson there is the construction of a building for troops, $110,000; at Whitehorse, there is another building, $180,000. As the hon. member will see, out of a total increase of $3,658,000, $3,281,000 is this year being spent to complete work that was started last year.
Subitem agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The next is Royal Canadian Air Force, subitems 1 to 21, $90,074,612.
Royal Canadian Air Force (Regular) -
Civil salaries and wages, $12,554,139; civilian allowances, $253,135; pay and allowances, $66,003,768; travelling and removal expenses, $6,852,014; freight, express and cartage, $4,307,300; pensions, superannuation and other benefits in respect of personal services, $104,256; total, $90,074,612.

In connection with this
there is a newspaper item which reads:
Airline Named to Operate Calgary Depot
Calgary, May 3. The operation of R.C.A.F. No. 10 repair depot at Currie Field, Calgary, will be taken over by Canadian Pacific Airlines, June 15, at the request of the defence department.
Will the minister tell us why that action was taken? On what basis is the operation of this No. 10 repair depot to be conducted by Canadian Pacific Air Lines?

We are making arrangements with a number of contractors to maintain and repair R.C.A.F. aircraft on much the same basis as was done during the war. Hon. members will recall Canadian Pacific Air Lines did this job to a considerable extent across the country. We have made arrangements whereby the contractor will lease the building and equipment and do the job of maintaining and repairing aircraft on a contract basis.
Is the reason for that the fact that the air force has not got the repair men who can do the job, and therefore they have to call in these outside contractors?

This is part of the policy of using civilian contractors wherever it is possible, and where the facilities are not needed for service purposes. If we had air force ground crews to do the job we would use them, but at the present time we will be needing all the facilities we can provide through contracts of this kind and ground crews we can recruit and train to meet the program.

Can the minister tell us whether the air force personnel at No. 10 repair depot has been moved or will be moved, or whether it will be an entirely civilian station or a combination of air force personnel and C.P.A. personnel?
There will be a nucleus of service personnel. It is a temporary arrangement and we expect it may last two years. By that time we shall have overtaken other obstacles, and it will have to be reviewed.

Where in the estimates is
payment provided for these contracts? I have looked through them fairly carefully but I cannot see anything in the nature of a contract for the repair of aircraft. Where in the estimates is that covered?
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I have with me a file concerning a French Canadian with 80709-305J
Supply-National Defence thirteen years' service in the air force. He is Flight Lieutenant J. J. Desrochers, regimental number 857.
Some time ago I stated that my compatriots of French origin were not treated with the fairness and respect to which they are entitled by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). The minister replied that he would strive to promote French Canadians who, apart from being bilingual, had the qualifications required.
I was therefore very much surprised to learn about the following facts that I wish to submit to the consideration of the house. Airman Desrochers writes as follows:
On July 4, 1938, having received my B.A. from Laval, I enlisted in the R.C.A.F. as pilot officer, in the permanent force. I shall not give you in detail the history of my military career as supply officer in this service in Canada and overseas. I will point out only that in 1940 1 was not only working to weaken the German effort threatening our rights but to protect the sacred rights of the French tongue.
I paid dearly for my daring. The rank of flight lieutenant I received on May 1, 1940, was my last promotion. From 1942 to October 24, 1950, everyone of my chiefs complained about my services, I had not initiative, I made too many routine mistakes, etc., etc. I fought valiantly but I could not win because I was the only French Canadian in the supply section of the general staff. On July 6, 1950,
I was dismissed on the pretext that I was unable to fulfil the requirements of the service, this after 13 years of service. What a joke I I took off His Majesty's nice blue uniform I had been wearing for thirteen years. As every employer to whom I applied would not believe that I had been discharged from the R.C.A.F. after so many years, without good reasons, as I was unable to find work commensurate with my ability, I had to work with a pick and shovel during the first months following my discharge.
I am sending you, sir, by registered letter, documentary evidence of the facts I have briefly stated in this letter, and I would ask you to be kind enough to return them after perusal.
When you read them, you will see that I have a good working knowledge of English, a prerequisite for advancement according to the hon. Mr. Claxton, who spoke so well when he said: "I assure the hon. member that if there are French-speaking officers who speak both languages, we push them ahead, etc., etc." I was pushed ahead so much, that I found myself on the street, with only a small pension as solace.
Let us now have a look at the actions of this man.
On September 28, 1941, he wrote Squadron Leader Lacoste, No. 3 training command, Montreal.
I would very much like to make you acquainted with the following facts which go once more to prove the oppression of which 1 told you, and which is the lot of a large number of French Canadians who, in good faith, have enlisted in our fine Royal Canadian Air Force.
R-127224, AC2 Marcel Lapointe, a French Canadian, tells me that on waking up this morning he naturally spoke in French to the fellow in the bed

Supply-National Defence next to his, a French Canadian too. Whereupon Corporal Duffield R-57893 came and upbraided him in these words: "Stop talking French at once or I'll report you to camp police! This is a Royal Canadian Air Force camp, and French is forbidden here!"
When you visited Moncton, I gave you a confidential letter which I had addressed to the officer commanding the camp, concerning a public notice prohibiting the use of French in the motor vehicle section.
The commanding officer had the notice removed but he did tell me that he recognized only the Canadian air force's language: English. He also pointed out that such an incident should simply have been reported to the officer commanding that section. I thought an incident of that nature, so dangerous for the relations between soldiers and non-commissioned officers of both races, should immediately be brought to the attention of the camp commandant.
You have approved of my actions and have asked me to inform you directly, in the future, of these unfortunate occurrences.
I am intelligent enough to realize that, by writing directly to headquarters, I am flying in the face of Royal Canadian Air Force rules and will probably run into trouble.
Jean-Jacques Desrochers, Flight Lieutenant.
Here is the document referred to in the preceding letter:
(Text):
To:	Commanding Officer,
No, 8 S.F.T.S.,
Moncton, N.B.
From: Senior Equipment Officer Subject: Personnel of French descent.
1.	It was reported to me yesterday, that on the blackboard of the mechanical transport section, the following order had been expressed in writing: English language only must be spoken around the M.T. section.
2.	I went last night to investigate the matter and saw that it was the truth: The word only had even been underlined twice. The only other language that can be spoken around the M.T. section besides the English language is the French language. Personnel employed in this particular section are as you know, of English descent or of French descent.
3.	I am inclined to believe that the non-commissioned officer in charge of the M.T. section must receive a wonderful co-operation from the French-Canadians working under him if he tolerates an order of such a pernicious nature to be written on his blackboard. The French-Canadians who were there at the time of my visit expressed their feelings very sharply against this oppression.
4.	There is nothing on earth more sacred to any individual, Englishman or Polish, Frenchman or Russian, etc. than his own language. It is the concrete expression of his patriotism. The actual struggle is against an enemy (Nazism) who wants to deprive each nation of this sacred right and also of religious freedom.
5.	It is a sacred duty for me as a French-Canadian officer to report to you, sir, the incident described above for your personal investigation.
Respectfully,
(J. J. Desrochers) FLT. LT.
Senior Equipment Officer No. 8 S.F.T.S.,
Moncton, N.B.

(Translation):
Two letters acknowledging receipt were forwarded to him. The first closed with the following:
Royal Canadian Air Force
Victoriaville, October 1, 1941
Rest assured that I share your views on all this and that I too must struggle fiercely enough to assert our rights. I must admit that here, thanks to a fair degree of co-operation, our people have little to complain about.
Your former assistant F/O Robinson has just joined us here, he speaks highly of you. Since I will necessarily be in close relationship with him, you would do me a good turn if you would advise me, if need be, as to the best way to deal with him in order to secure his fullest co-operation.
Yours very truly,
(Signed) C. E. Lacoste, F/Lt. Accountant Officer,
No. 3 I.T.S., R.C.A.F., Victoriaville, Que.
The second reads as follows:
(Text):
Montreal, October 23rd., 1941 FLT/LT J. J. Desrochers,
No. 8 E.F.T.S.,
R.C.A.F. Moncton, N.B.
My dear J.J.,
I received the letter which you addressed by error to Squadron Leader Lacoste. I can assure you that I immediately took the necessary action to have this matter investigated, and in so doing, did not implicate you in any manner.
1 thank you for passing this information on to me, and I request that you be good enough to inform me of any similar instances which may come to your knowledge in the future.
I can assure you that the authorities are in entire sympathy with all views concerning the subject named in your letter. May I further suggest, that whenever you become acquainted with cases of apparent delayed promotion, concerning French Canadian airmen, will you please inform the parties concerned of the means whereby this may be brought to the attention of their commanding officer. For the necessary action see K.R. (Air) Para. 439 and 439B.
I trust you are well and that all goes well with you.
Yours very truly,
M. Cantin, Squadron Leader.
(Translation):
It was after taking these steps to promote the recognition of the French language in the air force that airman Desrochers seems to have lost the confidence of his superiors. He began having troubles and difficulties. They wanted to compel him to resign and he was told so openly. On May 31, 1943, he wrote as follows:
(Text):
Montreal, P.Q., 31st of May 1943 Commanding Officer,
No. 12 (E) Depot,
Montreal East, P.Q.
I am No. C-857 Flight Lieutenant Jean-Jacques Desrochers, an officer of the permanent active air force commissioned in the said service since the 4th of July, 1938, and actually stationed at No. 12 equipment depot, Montreal East, P.Q.

On the 26th of May, 1943, at 11.30 a.m. I was paraded in your office by my adjutant Flight Lieutenant MacKeown where you gave me in substance the contents of a letter received from headquarters whereas my case had been studied particularly through my confidential reports and as a result I was considered below the average required from an officer holding the rank of Flight Lieutenant (I hold this rank since the 1st of May, 1940) but as my conduct and deportment had been good I was to be given the privilege of asking permission to resign my commission and in the case of my refusing, you were to take immediately the necessary procedure to have me retired from the service.
Strange as it may seem, after five years' service less one month, I was given approximately six hours to give a decision in this vital matter. Well,
I do not consider that applying to resign when I have not at all the intention of doing so and furthermore when I do not feel having deserved such an ultimatum is the right attitude to take in the matter as an officer of His Majesty's forces confident of doing and of having done his duty in the service. So, I hereby protest, giving briefly a short review of my service career, supported by exhibits when required. That, in accordance with K.R. Air Para. 255 Sub. Para. 4.
In January, 1939, I passed the British civil service commission interpreter's exams (English and French) obtaining 167 marks out of a possible 220 marks.
In February, 1939, I was posted on the equipment course given at R.C.A.F. station Trenton, Ont., with four other officers. In the middle of this seven months' duration course, I was sent on temporary duty to M.D. No. 4 in Quebec City with a French Canadian N.C.O. as recruiting officer for the R.C.A.F. Being only two, there is no need to say there was an excessive amount of work to do there.
I was away from my course two months and a half and was finally replaced in Quebec by Pilot Officer Emond. Notwithstanding the fact that I had been away from the course more than two months, I succeeded in my final exams obtaining 69 per cent of the total marks.
From now on, I am an equipment officer and my career really starts.
After my graduation, in September 1939, I was posted with No. 8 (BR) Squadron. This squadron had been sent from Rockcliffe air station, Ottawa, to the coast. So, I stayed three weeks in Rockcliffe and went down to Sydney, Nova Scotia.
I had no practical experience in my trade, having just completed the course and the organization of the equipment section and the supply problems met there were hard to solve due to the very restricted powers of purchase. Wartime financial regulations were not effective yet. Furthermore, the accountant branch had not yet been formed and I was equipment and accountant officer at the same time holding a flight lieutenant's position on the establishment of the squadron with the rank of pilot officer.
While on the strength of this squadron, I was promoted to the rank of flying officer. After seven months of unrelentless work I was replaced by flying officer Mchilney and posted to No. 1 (CAC) squadron. Saint John, New Brunswick. My commanding officer in Sydney, Squadron Leader Brown (now group captain) mentioned on my confidential report that I was a hard worker which pleased me because the staff and I had done a hard job under hard conditions.
At Saint John, New Brunswick, Flying Officer Labelle (now squadron leader) who had just completed his equipment course was posted with me under instructions. This officer now senior to me
Supply-National Defence in rank has been pleased to give me in a letter (see exhibit "A") his opinion looking back at the time he was a flying officer and I a flight lieutenant. I was promoted to the rank of flight lieutenant while at that station which was under the command of Squadron Leader A. Raymond now group captain, commanding officer of No. 2 S.F.T.S., Uplands, Ontario.
I was given a good confidential report by Squadron Leader Raymond and when it was decided to open No. 4 Manning Depot, Quebec City, Squadron Leader Raymond at the time who had been posted there at the opening recommended my posting at that new station.
I organized the equipment section at No. 4 Manning Depot. Posted there around the 1st of September, 1940, on the 5th of November of the same year I was chosen as officer commanding advance party going to open No. 8 S.F.T.S., Moncton, New Brunswick. Squadron Leader Raymond tried to delay my posting but I had to go there immediately.
This station, No. 8 S.F.T.S. was not yet completed. The contractors were still working. I will not emphasize on the hard conditions of work met there during the first month before the arrival of the commanding officer and the main staff. I kept the morale of my men high and obtained from them a maximum of efforts. Let me mention that Flying Officer Robertson posted as my assistant at that station and myself had to work all day, during the first two or three weeks unloading freight cars doing our administrative work only at night in order to cope with the receipts at the beginning.
I am pleased to produce (see exhibit "B") an article published in the "Take-Off" in November, 1942, where the early days of this station are remembered in a true and original way.
I held the position of senior equipment officer in Moncton during fifteen months. This position called for a squadron leader as per establishment. At my departure, on posting to No. 12 equipment depot the commanding officer of the station Wing Commander Brown took the occasion of a mess dinner to mention to all the officers the good work I had done as the first officer posted to No. 8 S.F.T.S. and up to my actual posting to No. 12 (E) depot.
Regardless of all this, I did not receive good reports while at that station. I tried to fight against an anti-French feeling which existed at that station. During all my service with the R.C.A.F. I fought for the respect and the rights of my compatriots and of the French language.
At Moncton, I reported two incidents to the commanding officer: (a) The first one, was the case of No. R127224, AC2 M. Lapointe who, one morning having addressed his bed neighbour, a French-Canadian in French was told by the N.C.O. in charge of the hut that he would report him to the service police of the station if he would use French again. On that instance, the commanding officer reprimanded the N.C.O. in question who was No. R57893 Corporal Duffield. (b) Two, the second was reported to the commanding officer in writing (see exhibit "C"). The pernicious notice was removed upon the commanding officer's order but a stormy interview resulted. I was told that I was very hot about things of that nature and that I was at fault in writing directly to the commanding officer and that in fact the N.C.O. in charge had the right to run his own section.
Finally Wing Commander Brown told me that he had the notice removed but that as far as he was concerned he recognized only one language: the language of the R.C.A.F.
At that moment I knew I was at the wrong door. I wrote to command headquarters and finally got the assurance that the authorities were in full

Supply-National Defence
sympathy with me and that action was taken to prevent any further incident. See exhibits (c) and (d).
What happened? Three months after I am posted to No. 12 (E) depot and this is important to note. After having kept a position of squadron leader during fifteen months I am given a flight lieutenant's position on the establishment of No. 12 (E) depot.
After ten months, around December, 1943, the commanding officer, Wing Commander Wilkins paraded me in his office and after a review of my file told me he would recommend me for the rank of acting Squadron Leader. I did not hear about that till after he left for England when Wing Commander A. H. Mielke paraded me in his office and showed me a report that had already gone to headquarters and back with a letter where he was requested to show me the report so that I could see where my weaknesses were.
Although I was recommended for the promotion I was amazed and depressed at the same time to read that I had trouble to express myself clearly in English and that my posting to a bilingual station was recommended. (Note that 80 per cent approximately of the civilian employees at this depot are of French descent). Note also that I was given 10 official R.C.A.F. investigations, in each case an interpreter would have been needed.
There is no need to say any more to try to explain, it is evident that I am not wanted. The three last monthly confidential reports are not in my favour. It is a fact that from their reading one cannot think that they are such as to determine the authorities to dismiss an officer from the service unless this officer can compare such reports with the ones prepared for his fellow officers.
I will now conclude this already too long report in which I have honestly and sincerely explained my situation and my feelings. As a permanent active air force officer who has been through in his trade the hard periods of organization of the B.C.A.T.P., I protest against a retirement.
(J. J. Desrochers) Flight Lieutenant, No. 12 Equipment Depot,
Montreal East, P.Q.

1.	In accordance with the provisions of AFAO P3/6 Part III paragraph 10, I have read carefully the report made by the AOC AMC in his letter file C-857 (AOC) dated 29 Sept. 1949, on my activities and achievements in the capacity of supply officer at AMC. This report was made following the receipt of an assessment made by my immediate superior S/L M. A. Rosenthal, on myself, on the 31st August, 1949.
(Mr. Gagnon.]
2.	It may be noted that in January, 1949, my whole career had been reviewed closely by the AOC AMC who had made at that time a recommendation for my retention in the service on an R211 dated 21 Jan. 49.
3.	I will not go further into the past as the main purpose of this statement is to express my disagreement on the present report both in principle and in fact.
4.	In principle, my contention is that an officer who has been holding the position and taking the responsibilities such as I have been holding and taking over the past seven months cannot be a man who is, has or shows at the same time as the case may be:
(a)	A weak character
(b)	A lack of aggressiveness
(c)	A passive attitude towards his career
(d)	A poor self-defence
(e)	Ineffective
(f)	Unproductive
(g)	A poor organizer
(h)	Mentally and psychologically incapable
(i)	No initiative
(j)	No ambition
(k)	No ability to improve
(l)	No logic
5.	I regret to say that the above is the moral picture of 857 F/L JJ Desrochers as is found in the above mentioned report. Of course my verdict is subject to caution but I am wholly in favour of referring this question to a psychiatrist and accepting his decision.
(Translation):
I shall not read further from this letter. May I in conclusion say this:
These were the excuses given for the dismissal of Desrochers, after 13 years of continuous service. He was not accused of having failed in his duty on a specific date; he was accused merely of general deficiencies of character which have not been proven at all.
If these deficiencies did exist, why was he kept so long in the air force?
I am inclined to believe, in spite of what the minister may think, that Desrochers was a victim of his devotion to the French-Cana-dian people, his compatriots, and that he paid with his position his love for his people. A thorough and impartial investigation should be made in this matter and I would ask the the minister to have it carried out.
Need I say that facts like these, when they are known, turn the French-Canadian away from a military career?
The best publicity that could be done by the Department of National Defence among the people of Quebec would be to place recruits in a friendly and sympathetic atmosphere. They are entitled to receive orders and training in their own language. Let us recognize that privilege. Upon it rests the future and success of our fighting men in training camps as well as on the battlefield.

Just a word, Mr. Chairman. Officers guilty of resorting to such methods should be cashiered.
